Droplets must be collected immediately using an amalgamating copper coil, mercury collector bulb, or dusted with flowers of sulfur/zinc powder.

3. Comprehensive Chemical Safety & Incompatibility Registry (Monica Chart 3.3)

Master reference of common laboratory reagents, their primary chemical hazards, flash points, incompatibilities, and imperative handling precautions.

Reagent / Chemical Flash Point / Physical State Primary Health & Physical Hazards Incompatible Reagents & Storage Rules
Acetic Acid (Glacial) 40°C • Liquid (freezes at 16.6°C) Corrosive, causes severe burns, pungent irritating fumes. Flammable. Keep away from oxidizers (nitric acid, chromic acid, peroxides, permanganates). Protect eyes, skin, and respiratory tract.
Acetone −18°C • Volatile liquid Extremely flammable and volatile. Vapors irritate eyes and mucous membranes. Keep away from ignition sources, chloroform, sulfuric acid, nitric acid, and strong oxidizers. Use in well-ventilated areas.
Ammonia Solution (Conc.) Pungent gas in aqueous solution Corrosive to tissues. Intense respiratory and ocular irritant. Liberates $NH_3$ gas. Place cloth over cap before opening to catch spray. Keep away from mercury and halogens (chlorine, iodine). Fume cupboard recommended.
Barium Chloride Solid white crystals Toxic if ingested or inhaled. Irritates skin and gastrointestinal mucosa. Store in locked cupboard. Protect against ingestion, dust inhalation, and dermal contact.
Calcium Hypochlorite (Bleach powder) Solid powder / granules Corrosive, oxidizing. Contact with acids liberates deadly toxic chlorine gas ($Cl_2$). Keep tightly sealed away from acids, moisture, flammable solvents, and organic matter.
Chloroform Volatile liquid • Non-flammable Harmful if ingested or inhaled. Suspected carcinogen and hepatotoxin. Anesthetic vapor. Avoid breathing vapor. Use in fume cupboard. Decomposes into toxic phosgene gas ($COCl_2$) in open flame. Protect skin.
Chromic Acid (Cleaning solution) Liquid solution (Dichromate in $H_2SO_4$) Extremely corrosive causing deep ulcerating burns. Powerful oxidizer and proven carcinogen. Keep strictly isolated from combustible organic materials, acetone, ethanol, and reducing agents.
DPX Mountant Liquid resin (contains Xylene) Highly flammable (FP 25°C). Irritating to eyes, skin, and lungs. Chronic neurotoxicity. Keep away from flames and sparks. Work in ventilated room. Do not pour solvent waste into sinks.
Diethyl Ether −40°C • Highly volatile liquid Extremely flammable. Forms explosive organic peroxides on light exposure. Anesthetic vapor. Opaque amber container, never rubber liners. Keep away from oxidizers, halogens, and sparks. Discard after 1 yr. Spark-proof fridge only.
Ethanol / Methanol 12°C • Volatile liquids Highly flammable. Methanol is toxic if ingested (metabolized to formic acid → blindness/death). Keep in dedicated flammables cupboard. Extinguish burners. Wash hands immediately after handling methanol.
Formaldehyde (Formalin 37–40%) Pungent liquid / gas solution Toxic, corrosive, severe mucous membrane irritant. Potent allergen, sensitizer, and human carcinogen. Use strictly in fume cupboard. Keep away from $HCl$ (forms bis-chloromethyl ether, a potent carcinogen). Do not store below 21°C (forms paraformaldehyde precipitate).
Hydrochloric Acid (37% Conc.) Fuming liquid Corrosive, causes severe chemical burns. Choking, highly irritating hydrogen chloride fumes. Use in fume cupboard. Dilute via AAW rule. Store on low shelves away from strong alkalis, cyanide, and hypochlorites.
Hydrogen Peroxide (≥30%) Colorless liquid Corrosive to skin (bleaching/blistering). Strong oxidizer; explosive decomposition if contaminated. Store in opaque vented container in cool dark area away from organic flammables, metals, and reducing agents.
Iodine (Crystals & Lugol's) Violet-black solid / solution Harmful by inhalation and skin contact. Irritating vapor. Sublimes readily at ambient temp. Store in amber glass bottles. Never use rubber-lined caps (iodine degrades rubber). Reacts violently with ammonia and acetylene.
Mercuric Chloride ($HgCl_2$) Heavy white powder Extremely toxic if swallowed or absorbed. Nephrotoxic and neurotoxic. Severe environmental toxin. Store in locked POISONS cupboard. Handle with spatulas and nitrile gloves. Dispose via hazardous waste protocols.
Nitric Acid (70% Conc.) Fuming oxidizing liquid Extremely corrosive (yellow skin staining via xanthoproteic reaction). Strong oxidizer; releases toxic $NO_2$ gas in fires. Store separately from organic acids (acetic) and flammable solvents. Dilute via AAW rule. Never mix with ethanol.
Phenol (Carbolic acid) Pink/white crystals or liquid Highly toxic, readily absorbed through intact skin causing extensive painless deep burns and systemic collapse. Wear thick neoprene gloves and eye shields. Wash splashes immediately with copious water or polyethylene glycol (PEG). Keep away from oxidizers.
Picric Acid (Wet solid) Yellow crystalline paste Explosive when dry. Forms shock-sensitive explosive salts with copper, lead, iron, and concrete. Store submerged under >30% water layer. Submerge dry containers overnight before opening. Amber glass/plastic bottles only.
Potassium Cyanide ($KCN$) White crystalline solid Deadly poison. Contact with any acid liberates lethal hydrogen cyanide gas ($HCN$). Store in locked POISONS cupboard. Mandatory logbook. Treat spills with alkaline ferrous sulfate to detoxify to ferrocyanide.
Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$) Deep purple crystalline solid Powerful oxidizer. Contact with organic flammables, glycerol, or concentrated acids causes violent explosion. Store in cool dry cupboard away from combustible materials, glycerol, alcohols, and concentrated acids.
Sodium Hydroxide Pellets ($NaOH$) White deliquescent pellets Extremely corrosive, causes severe caustic eye damage and deep skin ulcerations. Highly exothermic dissolution. Deliquescent: keep tightly capped. Welds glass stoppers shut; use plastic/rubber stoppers. Add slowly to water with continuous stirring.
Sulphuric Acid (98% Conc.) Dense oily liquid Intensely corrosive, powerful dehydrating agent causing rapid tissue charring and immense heat on water contact. Strict AAW dilution law. Store in lower plastic tray away from chlorates, permanganates, and water.
Xylene 25°C • Aromatic liquid Flammable liquid and vapor. CNS depressant, respiratory irritant, causes defatting dermatitis. Store in flammables cabinet. Avoid skin contact and inhalation. Keep away from strong oxidizers and naked flames.

4. Chemical Spillage Control & Decontamination Protocols

District laboratories must maintain an emergency Chemical Spill Kit containing sodium bicarbonate, soda ash, dilute acetic acid, flowers of sulfur, activated charcoal, vermiculite/sand, absorbent pads, heavy neoprene gloves, and full polycarbonate safety goggles.

Spill Classification Immediate First Action Neutralization / Absorption Agent Final Cleanup & Waste Handling
Concentrated Mineral Acid Spills ($HCl, H_2SO_4, HNO_3$) Evacuate immediate area, put on heavy neoprene gloves, face shield, and rubber apron. Neutralize cautiously by encircling and covering with Sodium Bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) or soda ash until effervescence ($CO_2$ bubbling) ceases. Mop up neutralized slurry with water, absorb on vermiculite/sand, and flush residual surface with excess water down chemical drain.
Caustic Alkali Spills ($NaOH, KOH, NH_4OH$) Isolate area, wear chemical-resistant gloves and goggles. Neutralize with Dilute Acetic Acid (5% vinegar) or Boric Acid powder until neutral pH is reached. Absorb with paper towels or sand, collect in plastic waste bag, and wash floor thoroughly with water and detergent.
Volatile Flammable Solvents (Ether, Acetone, Xylene, Alcohols) Instantly extinguish all open flames, isolate gas mains, avoid operating electrical switches (to prevent sparks), and open exterior windows for maximal ventilation. Cover spillage with Activated Charcoal, Vermiculite, Sand, or specialized Spill Pillows. Do NOT use flammable sawdust. Collect using non-sparking plastic scoops into a sealed airtight container or metal bucket. Dispose of via regulated incineration or hazardous burial. Never use a standard electric vacuum cleaner.
Cyanide Solution Spills ($KCN, NaCN$) Evacuate room, wear full respiratory apparatus and heavy gloves. Prevent any acid contact. Treat with a freshly mixed solution of Ferrous Sulphate ($FeSO_4$) made alkaline with Sodium Hydroxide or Alkaline Sodium Hypochlorite to oxidize cyanide to non-toxic cyanate. Allow 30 minutes reaction time, mop up oxidized non-toxic residue, and flush down drain with copious running water.
Elemental Mercury Spills (Broken Thermometer) Ventilate room immediately to disperse toxic heavy metal vapors. Evacuate pregnant staff. Coalesce droplets using an amalgamating copper spiral/wire or mercury collector sponge. Dust residual inaccessible cracks with Flowers of Sulfur or Zinc Dust to form non-volatile mercury sulfide/amalgam. Transfer collected mercury into a sealed polyethylene bottle covered with water. Bury in a deep covered pit or return to national chemical recycling center.

5. Safety Guidelines for Compressed and Liquefied Gas Cylinders

  • Mechanical Restraint: Gas cylinders (LPG, oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen) must always be securely chained or strapped upright in sturdy metal racks to prevent falling and fracturing the high-pressure valve stem (which turns the cylinder into an unguided rocket).
  • Valve Stem Protection: When moving cylinders, always fit the steel protective valve cap. Move cylinders exclusively on dedicated wheeled cylinder trolleys; never roll cylinders horizontally across the floor.
  • Leak Detection Law: Test all cylinder valves, regulator couplings, and hose connections using soapy water solution or liquid leak detector (bubbles indicate escaping gas). NEVER test for gas leaks using a naked flame or lit match.
  • Storage Location: Store spare cylinders in an external, well-ventilated, weather-protected, lockable gas cage outside the laboratory building, away from direct sunlight, corrosive vapours, and combustible vegetation.
Section 3.4 Interactive Board Examination (8 MCQs)
LEVEL 1 • FLAMMABLE HAZARDS & FLASH POINTS Q-ID: 3.4.01
A district laboratory uses diethyl ether for lipid extraction and fecal parasite concentration. Which statement accurately describes the physicochemical hazards and mandatory storage protocols for diethyl ether?
A It has a flash point of −40°C and may form shock-sensitive explosive peroxides on light exposure; it must be stored in spark-proof refrigerators or dark amber bottles without rubber-lined caps.
B It has a flash point of +40°C, making it safe to store in standard domestic refrigerators as long as the door gasket is intact.
C It is a non-volatile liquid that should be sealed tightly with natural rubber stoppers to prevent evaporation into the laboratory.
D It poses an environmental threat but no physical explosive or fire hazard under tropical ambient temperatures.
Option A (CORRECT): Diethyl ether has an exceptionally low flash point (−40°C) and auto-oxidizes in light/air to form detonating organic peroxides. It must be kept in opaque amber containers (no rubber liners, as ether dissolves rubber) and stored exclusively in spark-proof fridges or dedicated flammables cabinets.
Option B: Glacial acetic acid has a flash point of 40°C, not ether. Storing ether in domestic fridges causes vapor pooling and thermostat spark explosions.
Option C: Ether is highly volatile and vigorously degrades natural rubber liners and stoppers.
Option D: Ether represents one of the most volatile, extreme fire and explosion hazards in the laboratory.
LEVEL 1 • EXPLOSIVES: PICRIC ACID HYDRATION Q-ID: 3.4.02
While inspecting a legacy reagent storage room, a laboratory technologist discovers an old bottle of crystalline Picric Acid (trinitrophenol) where all surface liquid has evaporated and dry crystals line the bottle neck and cap threads. What is the mandatory and safe procedure to manage this container?
A Firmly unscrew the bottle cap over a sink and rapidly pour hot tap water inside to rehydrate the crystals.
B Never unscrew the cap or strike the bottle; submerge the unopened container into a bucket of water overnight, then gently loosen the cap underwater wearing eye protection and refill with distilled water.
C Scrape the dried crystals out using a metal stainless steel spatula and dissolve them in concentrated hydrochloric acid.
D Transfer the dry bottle directly into an autoclave to melt and sterilize the contents at 121°C for 15 minutes.
Option A: Unscrewing the dry cap creates mechanical friction across crystalline picric acid trapped in the screw threads, which can trigger an instantaneous fatal detonation.
Option B (CORRECT): Dry picric acid is friction- and shock-sensitive. The standard procedure is to submerge the unopened container upright in a water bucket overnight to allow water to penetrate capillary spaces in the cap, loosen the cap underwater with protective gear, and top up with water so the solid remains >30% hydrated.
Option C: Scraping with metal spatulas produces friction and forms highly sensitive metallic picrates.
Option D: Autoclaving dry trinitrophenol will result in a catastrophic bomb explosion inside the autoclave.
LEVEL 1 • CORROSIVES & AAW DILUTION LAW Q-ID: 3.4.03
A laboratory assistant needs to prepare 500 mL of 10% v/v Sulphuric Acid ($H_2SO_4$) from a stock bottle of 98% concentrated sulphuric acid. Which preparation technique strictly prevents violent acid spattering and container breakage?
A Pour 50 mL of concentrated acid into an empty beaker, then rapidly squirt 450 mL of cold distilled water directly on top of the acid.
B Measure 450 mL of cold distilled water into a borosilicate flask, and slowly pour 50 mL of concentrated sulphuric acid down the flask side while continuously mixing.
C Heat the concentrated acid on a hot plate to 80°C before mixing with boiling water to equalize temperatures.
D Combine concentrated acid and water in a closed polyethylene bottle and shake vigorously for 30 seconds.
Option A: Violates the AAW Rule (Always Add Acid to Water). Water added to dense acid forms a localized superheated layer that boils violently, propelling corrosive acid into the face.
Option B (CORRECT): The AAW Rule mandates adding concentrated acid slowly into a large volume of water with continuous stirring in heat-resistant borosilicate glass, allowing the large heat capacity of water to dissipate the massive exothermic hydration energy safely.
Option C: Pre-heating concentrated sulphuric acid dramatically escalates thermal stress and explosive boiling hazards.
Option D: Shaking in a sealed plastic bottle will melt the bottle from hydration heat and blow the cap off under intense pressure.
LEVEL 1 • CAUSTIC ALKALIS & STOPPER INCOMPATIBILITIES Q-ID: 3.4.04
Why is the use of ground-glass stoppers strictly forbidden for reagent bottles containing concentrated Sodium Hydroxide ($NaOH$) or Potassium Hydroxide ($KOH$) solutions?
A Ground glass catalyzes the reduction of sodium hydroxide into explosive metallic sodium.
B Strong alkalis attack and dissolve silica glass to form sodium silicate ($Na_2SiO_3$), which fuses and permanently cements the glass stopper shut.
C Ground glass absorbs moisture from the alkali, creating an exothermic fire inside the stopper joint.
D Glass stoppers turn basic solutions acidic within 24 hours of contact.
Option A: Alkalis do not reduce to metallic sodium in aqueous solutions.
Option B (CORRECT): Strong caustic alkalis slowly react with the silica ($SiO_2$) in glass, producing sodium silicate ("water glass"), an adhesive cement that permanently locks and freezes ground-glass stoppers. Polyethylene, polypropylene, or rubber stoppers must always be used.
Option C: Glass does not absorb moisture to produce fires.
Option D: Glass dissolution does not neutralize or acidify strong bases.
LEVEL 2 • EMERGENCY ACID SPILL NEUTRALIZATION Q-ID: 3.4.05
A 2.5-liter Winchester bottle of concentrated Hydrochloric Acid ($HCl, 37\%$) slips from a bench-level tray, shattering on the tile floor. Pungent, choking acidic fumes fill the room. Which step-by-step sequence must the laboratory health and safety team execute immediately?
A Evacuate room personnel, don respirator, heavy neoprene gloves, and eye visor; encircle and neutralize the spill with sodium bicarbonate or soda ash until effervescence ceases, absorb with sand/vermiculite, and mop with excess water.
B Pour 5 liters of concentrated sodium hydroxide pellets directly onto the liquid acid to neutralize the pH instantly without generating carbon dioxide gas.
C Cover the acid pool with dry flammable sawdust, vacuum immediately with a standard hospital electric vacuum cleaner, and seal in paper bags.
D Pour 10,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite (bleach) over the hydrochloric acid to disinfect the spill area before cleaning.
Option A (CORRECT): Acid spills require immediate room evacuation, respiratory and skin PPE, neutralization with a mild buffering base like Sodium Bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) or soda ash (applied from perimeter inward until bubbling stops), followed by inert absorption (sand/vermiculite) and water washing.
Option B: Adding concentrated $NaOH$ pellets to concentrated $HCl$ triggers a violent, explosive exothermic acid-base reaction that spatters boiling acid and caustic liquor everywhere.
Option C: Sawdust is combustible and chars with concentrated acids; electric vacuums spark and corrode, presenting severe electrocution and fume release hazards.
Option D: Mixing bleach with hydrochloric acid liberates massive clouds of lethal Chlorine gas ($Cl_2$).
LEVEL 2 • TOXIC AZIDES & PLUMBING EXPLOSIONS Q-ID: 3.4.06
A district hospital laboratory routinely discards expired diagnostic blood grouping and chemistry reagents containing 0.1% Sodium Azide ($NaN_3$) directly down a sink fitted with antique copper and lead drainage pipes. Six months later, a plumber clearing a clogged trap with an auger triggers a violent explosion. What chemical reaction caused this blast?
A Sodium azide reacted with copper and lead in the pipes to form heavy metal azides (copper and lead azide), which are sensitive primary explosives detonated by mechanical shock.
B Sodium azide combined with drain water to liberate combustible pure propane gas inside the sink trap.
C Sodium azide dissolved the copper piping into toxic copper sulfate crystals that caught fire from air exposure.
D The plumber's mechanical snake created static electricity that ignited residual hydrogen peroxide in the drain.
Option A (CORRECT): Sodium azide reacts over time with copper, brass, and lead plumbing to accumulate metallic azides ($Cu(N_3)_2$, $Pb(N_3)_2$). These are extremely friction- and shock-sensitive primary explosives (chemically similar to detonator caps) that explode upon mechanical contact by plumbing tools. Reagents with azide must be flushed with huge water volumes or treated as hazardous waste.
Option B: Azides contain nitrogen ($N_3^-$), not hydrocarbons like propane.
Option C: Copper sulfate is a non-explosive, non-flammable blue salt.
Option D: The detonation is the classic, textbook consequence of metallic azide buildup in heavy metal pipes.
LEVEL 2 • TOXIC POISONS SECURITY & CYANIDE PROTOCOLS Q-ID: 3.4.07
A laboratory uses Potassium Cyanide ($KCN$) for preparing cyanmethemoglobin reagent (Drabkin's solution). Which security storage protocol, chemical incompatibility, and spillage detoxification rule is mandatory for this reagent?
A It must be kept in an open shelf next to dilute acids; spills should be neutralized by pouring glacial acetic acid over the powder.
B It must be secured in a locked POISONS cupboard with an inventory log; contact with acids liberates lethal Hydrogen Cyanide ($HCN$) gas, and spills must be detoxified using freshly prepared alkaline ferrous sulphate or alkaline hypochlorite.
C It can be safely poured down standard sinks because cyanide rapidly oxidizes to sugar in municipal sewage systems.
D Cyanide powder should be stored in an open glass dish inside a domestic refrigerator to keep the crystals cold.
Option A: Adding any acid (including acetic acid) to cyanide releases lethal gaseous $HCN$, causing rapid asphyxiation and death.
Option B (CORRECT): Potassium cyanide is an extreme poison requiring locked cupboard security and strict dispensing logs. In acidic conditions, it evolves toxic $HCN$ gas. Spills are chemically detoxified into harmless ferrocyanide by treatment with alkaline ferrous sulphate ($FeSO_4 + NaOH$) or oxidized to cyanate by alkaline hypochlorite.
Option C: Cyanide is highly lethal to aquatic life and must never be poured into drains without chemical detoxification.
Option D: Storing cyanide open in a domestic fridge creates extreme contamination and vapor hazards.
LEVEL 2 • MERCURY SPILLAGE & TOXIC VAPOR MITIGATION Q-ID: 3.4.08
A glass clinical thermometer breaks on the floor of an unventilated blood transfusion room, scattering tiny metallic mercury droplets into floor cracks. Which action represents the correct biosafety procedure to prevent chronic mercury toxicity among laboratory staff?
A Sweep the floor briskly with a dry broom and vacuum the dust with a standard domestic vacuum cleaner to blow the mercury into the vacuum bag.
B Open windows for maximal ventilation, evacuate pregnant personnel, collect visible droplets with a copper coil amalgamator or mercury sponge, dust inaccessible cracks with sulfur powder or zinc dust, and seal waste in a water-covered bottle for deep pit disposal.
C Pour concentrated nitric acid over the floor cracks to dissolve the mercury droplets into nitrogen dioxide gas.
D Ignore the droplets because elemental liquid mercury cannot evaporate at normal tropical room temperatures ($25^\circ ext{C}$).
Option A: Vacuuming mercury with a standard vacuum aerosolizes and vaporizes the mercury, blowing huge concentrations of toxic mercury vapor into the room air through the vacuum exhaust.
Option B (CORRECT): Mercury emits toxic vapors at ambient temperatures. Decontamination requires opening windows, collecting pools with an amalgamating copper wire/sponge, and treating inaccessible floor cracks with flowers of sulfur (forms non-volatile $HgS$) or zinc dust (forms solid zinc amalgam), sealing in a sealed container under water.
Option C: Nitric acid on mercury generates dense, deadly reddish-brown nitrogen dioxide ($NO_2$) gas.
Option D: Mercury has significant vapor pressure at room temperature and accumulates in human tissues, causing severe neurological and renal toxicity.
Master Overview › Chapter 3: Health and Safety › 3.5 Safe Handling & Storage of Chemicals
PART 1 • CHAPTER 3 • SUBUNIT 3.5

Safe Handling, Segregated Storage Architecture, Incompatibilities & Hazardous Waste Disposal

Book Pages: 81–86
Section 3.5 Core Examination Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 81–86)

Segregated Chemical Store Architecture

External, cool, well-ventilated storeroom with cross-ventilation. Flammable liquid cabinets must be fire-resistant steel with a 50 mm liquid-retaining sill (sump) at the bottom. Corrosive mineral acids stored on lowest shelving tiers (< 1 meter from floor) inside corrosion-proof plastic trays.

Strict Chemical Incompatibility Laws

Oxidizers (nitric acid, chromic acid, permanganates) must NEVER be stored with organic solvents (ethanol, acetone, ether, acetic acid). Acids must never touch cyanides (forms lethal $HCN$ gas) or bleach (forms toxic $Cl_2$ gas). Caustic alkalis must never be sealed with ground-glass stoppers.

Safe Transport, Dispensing & Metrology

Transport large glass reagent bottles (Winchester bottles, 2.5 L) exclusively inside padded double-walled bottle carriers—never by the neck alone. Dispense fuming acids, formalin, and volatile toxic solvents inside a certified chemical fume hood. Mouth-pipetting is strictly outlawed under criminal penalty.

Hazardous Chemical Waste & Neutralization

Mineral acid and alkali effluents must be neutralized to pH 6.5–8.5 and flushed with excess running tap water. Organic solvents collected in segregated solvent waste drums. Heavy metals (mercury, barium, silver) precipitated or buried in deep covered pits; never discarded into municipal sewers.

1. Chemical Storeroom Architecture & Environmental Specifications

According to Cheesbrough (p. 81), improper chemical storage in tropical district laboratories is a primary catalyst for laboratory fires, explosions, toxic fumes, and reagent spoilage. Chemical stores must adhere to four essential architectural mandates:

Chemical Class Mandatory Storage Location & Construction Shelving & Height Rules Specific Environmental Controls
Flammable & Volatile Solvents (Ether, Acetone, Methanol, Xylene) Dedicated heavy-gauge steel safety cabinet with double-walled construction, 3-point door latch, and 50 mm leak-tight bottom sill (sump). Shelves must have raised lip edges. Max volume on open bench: ≤ 500 mL. Store in coolest room zone away from sunlight. Strict ban on domestic refrigerators (explosion-proof/spark-proof fridges only).
Concentrated Mineral Acids ($HCl, H_2SO_4, HNO_3$) Dedicated acid-resistant cabinet or lower wooden/polypropylene shelving lined with heavy polyethylene containment trays. Lowest shelf only (< 1 meter from floor). Never store mineral acids above eye level or on high shelves. Well-ventilated with external draft vents. Separate nitric acid (oxidizer) from organic acids (glacial acetic acid).
Scheduled Poisons & Toxic Salts ($KCN, HgCl_2, BaCl_2$) Locked "POISONS" Cupboard with heavy steel padlock. Key held exclusively by the Laboratory Safety Officer (LSO). Eye-level locked cabinet with dedicated inner compartments for cyanides and heavy metal powders. Dry ambient conditions. Mandatory poison inventory ledger recording date, quantity dispensed, test name, and operator signature.
Strong Oxidizing Agents ($HNO_3, KMnO_4, H_2O_2 \ge 30\%$) Isolated cool, dark cabinet on non-combustible ceramic or glass trays. Mid-level shelving away from wooden floorboards or combustible partitions. Store completely isolated from flammable solvents, alcohols, glycerol, and paper archives.
Deliquescent & Hygroscopic Solids ($NaOH, KOH$, Stains) Airtight polyethylene containers with screw caps and inner plastic seals. Dry, humidity-controlled shelving away from wet sinks. Keep tightly sealed immediately after dispensing to prevent atmospheric moisture absorption and carbonation.

2. Master Chemical Incompatibility Matrix (Dangerous Combinations)

Certain laboratory chemicals react violently when mixed or stored in proximity, generating toxic gases, fires, or spontaneous explosions (Monica Cheesbrough p. 84).

Primary Chemical Incompatible Reagents / Substances Hazardous Reaction & Detrimental Consequence
Concentrated Mineral Acids ($HCl, H_2SO_4$) Caustic Alkalis ($NaOH, KOH$), Cyanides, Bleach (Hypochlorite), Sodium Azide Violent exothermic boiling; releases lethal Hydrogen Cyanide ($HCN$), deadly Chlorine gas ($Cl_2$), or explosive hydrazoic acid.
Nitric Acid ($HNO_3$, 70%) Ethanol, Methanol, Acetone, Glacial Acetic Acid, Organic Matter Violent spontaneous combustion and explosion; dense brown toxic Nitrogen Dioxide ($NO_2$) gas release.
Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$) Glycerol, Ethylene Glycol, Concentrated $H_2SO_4$, Alcohols Spontaneous ignition and explosive decomposition on contact with organic polyols.
Sodium Azide ($NaN_3$) Copper, Lead, Brass plumbing fixtures; Strong Acids Forms hyper-sensitive metallic azides ($Cu(N_3)_2, Pb(N_3)_2$) that detonate under mechanical pipe shock.
Ammonia Solution (Conc.) Iodine crystals, Chlorine bleach, Elemental Mercury Forms shock-sensitive explosive Nitrogen Triiodide ($NI_3$) and corrosive chloramine fumes.
Formaldehyde (Formalin 37–40%) Hydrochloric Acid ($HCl$), Oxidizers Reacts with $HCl$ vapor to generate bis-chloromethyl ether (BCME), a potent Category 1 human lung carcinogen.
Picric Acid (2,4,6-Trinitrophenol) Concrete floors, Lead/iron/copper metals, Reducing agents Forms sensitive, detonating calcium and metallic picrates. Detonates when dry.

3. Safe Reagent Dispensing, Handling Metrology & Personal Protection

  • Winchester Bottle Handling Law: 2.5 L glass Winchester bottles containing acids or solvents must never be lifted or transported by the neck alone. Always use a dedicated rubber or double-walled polypropylene Winchester bottle carrier with a sturdy handle and cushioning base.
  • Pipetting Safety Mandate: mouth pipetting is strictly prohibited for all liquids (toxic, corrosive, infectious, or even distilled water). Use rubber suction bulbs, pipette pumps, or calibrated automatic micropipettes with aerosol-barrier filter tips.
  • Chemical Fume Extraction: All manipulations involving fuming hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, concentrated ammonia, formalin, and organic solvent extractions (formol-ether) must be conducted inside a certified fume extraction cupboard with minimum face velocity of 0.5 m/s.
  • Personal Protective Gear: Heavy neoprene gloves for mineral acids; nitrile gloves for organic solvents and toxic powders; polycarbonate safety goggles with closed-in side shields; heavy-duty rubber aprons for bulk acid dilutions.

4. Hazardous Chemical Waste Disposal & Effluent Neutralization Hierarchy

District laboratories must minimize environmental contamination by strictly segregating, detoxifying, and treating chemical effluents before disposal (Cheesbrough pp. 84–86).

Waste Category Laboratory Origin Examples Mandatory Treatment & Neutralization Protocol Final Safe Disposal Route
Mineral Acid & Alkali Effluents Acid-alcohol decolorizers, Fouchet's reagents, Turk's fluid, spent cleaning acids Collect in plastic carboys. Neutralize acids with Sodium Bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) and alkalis with dilute acetic acid until pH 6.5–8.5 is confirmed by indicator paper. Flush down chemical sink with copious volumes of running tap water (1:50 dilution).
Flammable Organic Solvents Xylene (clearing), DPX mountant, Acetone, Diethyl ether waste Collect in designated, clearly labeled, grounded steel or amber glass solvent waste drums. Never pour into sinks or drains. Re-distill and recycle where possible, or transfer to regional hazardous waste high-temperature incineration facility.
Cyanide Reagent Effluents Spent Drabkin's cyanmethemoglobin solution Treat with freshly prepared Alkaline Ferrous Sulphate ($FeSO_4 + NaOH$) to convert free cyanide into non-toxic ferrocyanide $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$. Allow 30 minutes reaction time, then flush down drain with running water.
Heavy Metal Residues ($Hg, Ba, Ag$) Mercuric chloride fixatives (Zenker's), Barium chloride, Silver stains Precipitate silver as insoluble Silver Chloride ($AgCl$) using $NaCl$; precipitate barium as Barium Sulfate ($BaSO_4$). Collect precipitates for chemical recovery or seal in heavy polyethylene containers for deep covered pit burial.

5. Tropical Chemical Stock Control & Expiration Management

  • The FEFO / FIFO Rule: Rotate chemical stock using First-Expired, First-Out (FEFO). Mark delivery date and date of first unsealing on every bottle label.
  • Formalin Temperature Trap: Formaldehyde (37–40% formalin) must never be stored below 21°C (e.g. in air-conditioned cold rooms or refrigerators), as low temperatures cause irreversible polymerization into white, insoluble paraformaldehyde flakes, destroying fixative potency. Store at 21–25°C.
  • Deliquescent Pellet Maintenance: Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide pellets must have their bottle threads wiped clean of powder and sealed tightly with Parafilm or grease-free plastic caps to prevent ambient moisture liquification.
Section 3.5 Interactive Board Examination (8 MCQs)
LEVEL 1 • FLAMMABLE STORAGE ENGINEERING Q-ID: 3.5.01
According to standard laboratory health and safety architecture (Cheesbrough p. 81), what is the mandatory structural feature required at the bottom of a dedicated steel flammable liquids storage cabinet?
A An open drainage pipe connected directly to the hospital municipal sewer.
B A 50 mm liquid-tight raised sill (sump) designed to contain accidental bottle leaks and spillage inside the cabinet.
C An internal electrical heater to keep volatile solvents warm during tropical monsoons.
D Perforated wooden shelving to absorb volatile solvent fumes.
Option A: Direct drain connections allow hazardous flammables to flood the sewer, causing street-level explosive blasts.
Option B (CORRECT): Flammable cabinets must feature a liquid-tight bottom sump (raised sill of at least 50 mm) capable of retaining the contents of ruptured Winchester bottles, preventing flammable liquids from escaping across the floor.
Option C: Electrical heaters are dangerous ignition sources that trigger solvent explosions.
Option D: Wood is combustible and strictly forbidden inside flammable safety stores; heavy steel shelves are required.
LEVEL 1 • CORROSIVE ACID SHELVING RULES Q-ID: 3.5.02
What is the strict rule regarding the vertical shelving placement of concentrated mineral acid bottles ($HCl, H_2SO_4, HNO_3$) in district laboratory chemical stores?
A They must be stored on the highest shelf near the ceiling to keep them out of reach of junior staff.
B They should be placed on eye-level glass shelves directly above water baths.
C They must be stored on the lowest shelving tiers (< 1 meter from floor) inside corrosion-resistant polyethylene trays to prevent ocular/facial splash injuries during retrieval.
D They must be stored on metal wire racks directly in contact with galvanized steel.
Option A: High shelves are extremely dangerous; reaching overhead for heavy glass acid bottles leads to dropped containers and fatal facial/body acid burns.
Option B: Glass shelves can fracture under Winchester weight; water baths provide heat and moisture that degrade acid storage.
Option C (CORRECT): Mineral acids must strictly reside on low shelves (< 1 m from ground) inside plastic catchment trays, eliminating overhead lifting hazards and containing accidental leaks.
Option D: Acid fumes rapidly corrode galvanized steel, leading to structural shelf collapse.
LEVEL 1 • REAGENT STABILITY & FORMALIN TRAP Q-ID: 3.5.03
A laboratory technician decides to store stock bottles of 37–40% Formaldehyde (formalin) inside a 4°C refrigerator to preserve them. What detrimental chemical change occurs to the formaldehyde solution under this low temperature?
A Formaldehyde oxidizes into flammable ether gas, bursting the bottle.
B It undergoes irreversible polymerization, forming a dense white precipitate of paraformaldehyde and drastically reducing the effective fixative concentration.
C It freezes into explosive crystal needles that detonate upon warming.
D It turns strongly alkaline (pH > 12) within 48 hours.
Option A: Formaldehyde does not oxidize to ether.
Option B (CORRECT): Storing formaldehyde below 21°C causes rapid polymerization into insoluble white paraformaldehyde flakes. This precipitates active formaldehyde out of solution, ruining its tissue fixation capability. Formaldehyde must always be maintained at 21–25°C.
Option C: Paraformaldehyde is not an explosive crystal.
Option D: Formaldehyde slowly acidifies to formic acid over time, never becoming basic.
LEVEL 1 • CHEMICAL TRANSPORT SAFETY Q-ID: 3.5.04
What is the mandatory method for safely carrying a 2.5-liter glass Winchester bottle of concentrated Sulphuric acid from the central store to the laboratory bench?
A Grasp the bottle firmly by the glass neck with bare hands and walk briskly.
B Place the Winchester bottle inside a dedicated rubber or double-walled polypropylene bottle carrier with a sturdy carrying handle and padded base.
C Place the glass bottle loosely inside a cardboard box with used paper towels.
D Carry the bottle horizontally tucked under the arm to protect the cap.
Option A: Lifting heavy Winchester bottles (over 4 kg when full) by the neck can snap the glass neck or slip from greasy fingers, dropping concentrated acid onto the feet and legs.
Option B (CORRECT): Winchester bottles must always be transported in dedicated, impact-resistant, chemical-proof bottle carriers. The carrier supports the bottom weight and contains all acid if the bottle fractures.
Option C: Cardboard boxes easily collapse when wet and offer no chemical containment.
Option D: Horizontal carrying risks severe cap leakage and drops.
LEVEL 2 • CHEMICAL INCOMPATIBILITY EXPLOSIONS Q-ID: 3.5.05
In an effort to clean stained glassware, a student laboratory assistant mixes 100 mL of concentrated Nitric Acid ($HNO_3, 70\%$) with 100 mL of 95% Ethanol in a closed glass flask. Within 60 seconds, the mixture boils violently, turns deep brown, and detonates the flask. What chemical incompatibility caused this disaster?
A Nitric acid is a powerful oxidizer that violently oxidizes organic alcohols, triggering runaway exothermic gas generation ($NO_2, CO_2$) and explosive blast pressure.
B Ethanol neutralized the nitric acid into water, causing hydraulic implosion.
C Nitric acid extracted oxygen from the glass walls of the flask.
D The explosion was caused solely by static electricity from the student's lab coat.
Option A (CORRECT): Nitric acid is an aggressive oxidizing agent. Mixing it with organic solvents (ethanol, methanol, acetone, acetic acid) initiates an uncontrollable oxidation reaction that evolves dense toxic $NO_2$ gas, immense thermal energy, and rapid overpressure explosions. Oxidizers and organic flammables must never be combined or stored together.
Option B: Alcohols do not neutralize acids into water; they are fuel for oxidation.
Option C: Nitric acid does not extract oxygen from silicate glass.
Option D: The blast is a classic textbook chemical incompatibility reaction, not a static spark.
LEVEL 2 • HAZARDOUS CHEMICAL WASTE MANAGEMENT Q-ID: 3.5.06
A district hospital laboratory generates 5 liters of spent acid-alcohol decolorizer and sulfuric acid reagents each week. Which waste management protocol is environmentally safe and complies with WHO guidelines?
A Pour the concentrated acidic waste directly down the sink without running tap water.
B Collect acid waste in a dedicated plastic carboy, neutralize cautiously with sodium bicarbonate until effervescence ceases and pH 6.5–8.5 is confirmed, then flush down sink with running tap water.
C Mix the acid waste with sodium hypochlorite bleach before pouring into the hospital storm drain.
D Pour the acid waste into an open pit in the hospital garden.
Option A: Direct acid disposal corrodes plumbing pipes and contaminates municipal water systems.
Option B (CORRECT): Mineral acid waste must be collected in corrosion-resistant carboys, neutralized with mild buffering agents like Sodium Bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) until pH 6.5–8.5 is achieved, and then flushed down drains with excess water.
Option C: Mixing acid with bleach liberates lethal Chlorine gas ($Cl_2$).
Option D: Garden dumping causes severe groundwater contamination and toxic environmental damage.
LEVEL 2 • TOXIC FUME INTERACTION & CARCINOGENESIS Q-ID: 3.5.07
Why must bottles of Formaldehyde (formalin) and concentrated Hydrochloric Acid ($HCl$) never be stored together in the same unventilated storage cupboard?
A Their vapors combine to form harmless table salt and water.
B Their escaping vapors react spontaneously in air to synthesize bis-chloromethyl ether (BCME), a potent Category 1 human respiratory carcinogen.
C Hydrochloric acid neutralizes formaldehyde into solid sugar crystals.
D Formaldehyde turns hydrochloric acid into non-corrosive acetic acid.
Option A: They do not form table salt.
Option B (CORRECT): When formaldehyde ($HCHO$) vapor mixes with hydrogen chloride ($HCl$) vapor in ambient air, they spontaneously react to synthesize bis-chloromethyl ether (BCME), an extremely dangerous, proven human lung carcinogen. They must always be segregated.
Option C: Acid does not polymerize formaldehyde into sugar.
Option D: No acetic acid synthesis occurs.
LEVEL 2 • CYANIDE DETOXIFICATION CHEMISTRY Q-ID: 3.5.08
A district laboratory prepares 2 liters of Drabkin's cyanmethemoglobin reagent containing Potassium Cyanide ($KCN$). At the end of the month, 500 mL of expired reagent must be discarded. What is the mandatory detoxification procedure before drain disposal?
A Add freshly prepared alkaline ferrous sulphate solution ($FeSO_4 + NaOH$) to convert toxic cyanide into non-toxic ferrocyanide complex, allow 30 minutes reaction time, and flush with excess water.
B Add 50 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid to boil off the cyanide as gas out the window.
C Boil the solution on an open hot plate to evaporate the cyanide into the laboratory.
D Dilute 1:1 with domestic cooking oil and pour into the hospital garden.
Option A (CORRECT): Cyanide waste must never be discarded untreated. Adding ferrous sulphate under alkaline conditions converts free $CN^-$ ions into the stable, non-toxic hexacyanoferrate complex $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ (ferrocyanide), which is safe for drain disposal with water flushing.
Option B: Adding acid liberates lethal $HCN$ gas, creating an extreme inhalation hazard.
Option C: Boiling cyanide produces lethal toxic fumes.
Option D: Cooking oil does not detoxify cyanide and contaminates soil.
Master Overview › Chapter 3: Health and Safety › 3.6 Equipment & Glassware Hazards
PART 1 • CHAPTER 3 • SUBUNIT 3.6

Equipment Safety, Electrical Protection, Autoclave Thermodynamics & Glassware Maintenance

Book Pages: 86–90
Section 3.6 Core Board Examination Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 86–90)

Dual Electrical Protection Architecture

Laboratory electrical circuits must feature two distinct protection mechanisms: Circuit Breakers (protect wiring from overload/overheating fires) and Earth-Fault Interrupters (RCD / GFCI) (protect personnel from lethal electrocution by tripping instantly if leakage exceeds 30 mA). Strict ban on multi-adaptors and spliced cords.

Centrifuge Dynamics & Rotor Balancing

Centrifuge tubes must be paired by weight (matched within ±0.1 g) with opposing buckets placed diametrically. Never use cracked tubes. If breakage occurs: switch off motor immediately, keep lid closed for 30 minutes to allow aerosol droplet nuclei to settle, and decontaminate with 10,000 ppm chlorine or 1% Virkon.

Autoclave Pressure Steam Thermodynamics

Autoclaving operates at 121°C (15 psi / 15 psi Pressure">103 kPa pressure) for 15 minutes. Never open until the pressure gauge reads zero and temperature drops below 80°C. Opening prematurely causes superheated liquids to boil violently, shattering glass and scalding staff with explosive steam.

Glassware Safety & flame-smoothing

Inspect all tubes, pipettes, and flasks for chips and star-cracks. Chipped rims and sharp Pasteur pipette ends must be gently flame-smoothed in a Bunsen flame to melt sharp edges before reuse. Broken glass and needles discarded strictly into puncture-resistant sharps containers.

1. Electrical Safety, Earthing & Overload Prevention

According to Cheesbrough (p. 88), electrical faults are a major cause of laboratory fires and fatal electric shocks in tropical district hospitals with fluctuating voltage supplies.

Safety Mechanism Engineering Function & Operation Specific Hazard Prevented Mandatory Implementation Standard
Circuit Breakers Electromechanical switch that automatically interrupts current flow when circuit amperage exceeds the cable rating. Electrical overload, wiring overheating, and electrical wall insulation fires. Installed on the main laboratory distribution board with dedicated 15A/20A lines for heavy equipment.
Earth-Fault Interrupters (RCD / GFCI) Monitors balance between live and neutral currents; trips circuit within 30 milliseconds if current leaks to ground ($> 30 ext{ mA}$). Fatal human electrocution from touching faulty equipment casing while standing on damp floors. Fitted to all laboratory sub-circuits, particularly near sinks, water baths, and centrifuges.
Grounded (3-Pin) Outlets Provides low-resistance earthing path directing fault currents safely into the ground. Equipment casing becoming live at 220–240V during internal insulation breakdown. All equipment must use approved 3-pin earthed plugs. Strict ban on cutting off ground pins.
Cable & Multi-Adaptor Bans Eliminates temporary extension leads, frayed joints, and multi-socket adaptors. Loose contact overheating, sparking, and trip hazards over floor cables. Each piece of equipment must plug directly into a dedicated fixed wall outlet.

2. Centrifuge Rotor Dynamics, Critical Speeds & Aerosol Safety

Centrifuges generate immense centrifugal force ($> 2,000 imes g$). Mechanical failures or tube fractures during high-speed rotation represent extreme physical and biological hazards (Cheesbrough pp. 86–87).

  • Rotor Balancing Law: Opposite centrifuge buckets and tubes must be balanced in pairs by weight (matching within ±0.1 g using a balance). Imbalance creates severe rotational vibration that damages bearings, fractures rotors, and can throw the machine off the bench.
  • Sealed Safety Buckets: Infectious specimens (sputum, blood, CSF) must be spun in aerosol-tight sealed buckets fitted with transparent polycarbonate screw caps and O-rings.
  • The 30-Minute Post-Breakage Rule: If an abnormal sound indicates tube breakage, immediately turn off the power switch. Keep the lid closed for at least 30 minutes to allow infectious aerosol clouds to settle. Open wearing heavy gloves and mask, remove broken glass with forceps, soak buckets in 10,000 ppm chlorine or 1% Virkon for 30 minutes, and autoclave buckets before reuse.

3. Autoclave Thermodynamics, Pressure Seals & Thermal Protection

  • Standard Cycle Parameters: Moist heat steam sterilization operates at 121°C at 15 psi Pressure">103 kPa (15 psi) gauge pressure for 15 minutes.
  • Safety Valve & Interlock Checks: The pressure relief safety valve and lid rubber gasket must be inspected weekly. Test safety valve lever manually to verify that steam vents freely without jamming.
  • Liquid Boil-Over & Implosion Hazards: When autoclaving liquid media or waste bottles, caps must be loosened slightly to allow pressure equalization. Tight caps will cause glass bottles to burst under steam pressure.
  • Cool-Down Safety Law: Never release the steam exhaust valve rapidly after liquid cycles; rapid decompression causes liquids to boil explosively. Never open the autoclave lid until the pressure gauge reads ZERO and the chamber temperature is below 80°C.

4. Glassware Inspection, Decontamination & flame-smoothing Technique

Damaged glassware is the leading cause of cut injuries and accidental blood inoculations in district laboratories (Cheesbrough p. 89).

Glassware Type Common Defect & Hazard Maintenance / Remediation Technique Disposal Criteria
Serological & Graduated Pipettes Chipped tips causing inaccurate volumetric delivery and finger lacerations; blocked capillary tips. flame-smoothing: Rotate chipped tip in the outer blue cone of a Bunsen flame for 5–10 seconds until glass edges melt smooth without constricting the bore. Discard into puncture-resistant container if tip bore is deformed or volume graduations are illegible.
Test Tubes & Centrifuge Tubes Chipped rims, hairline body cracks, and star-fractures that burst under centrifugal force. Flame-smooth slightly chipped rims. Discard any tube with visible stress fractures immediately. Never centrifuge cracked tubes. Discard in sharps container.
Volumetric Flasks & Cylinders Thermal stress fractures from heating over direct flame (volumetric glassware must NEVER be heated directly). Wash with mild detergent, rinse with deionized water, and air-dry at room temperature. Discard if chipped or cracked. Re-calibrate if exposed to extreme heat.
Microscope Slides & Cover Glasses Broken corners, razor-sharp shards, greasy bio-films. Soak reusable slides in 1,000 ppm chlorine or detergent; rinse and store in 70% alcohol. Discard broken slides into puncture-resistant sharps box. Never press cover slips with bare fingers.
Section 3.6 Interactive Board Examination (8 MCQs)
LEVEL 1 • ELECTRICAL SAFETY & RCD PROTECTION Q-ID: 3.6.01
What is the specific life-saving function of an Earth-Fault Interrupter (Residual Current Device / GFCI) in a medical laboratory electrical circuit?
A It prevents the laboratory voltage from rising above 220V during lightning storms.
B It protects personnel from fatal electrocution by tripping the electrical circuit within milliseconds if a leakage current to ground exceeds 30 mA.
C It converts alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC) for microscope light bulbs.
D It automatically recharges laboratory backup batteries when power fails.
Option A: Surge protectors manage voltage spikes, not earth-fault interrupters.
Option B (CORRECT): Earth-fault interrupters (RCDs/GFCIs) detect imbalances between live and neutral currents caused by current leaking through a human body to ground, tripping the circuit within 30 ms (>30 mA leakage) to prevent ventricular fibrillation and fatal electric shock.
Option C: AC/DC rectifiers convert current, not safety interrupters.
Option D: Inverters and UPS units manage battery charging.
LEVEL 1 • CENTRIFUGE SAFETY & AEROSOL CONTAINMENT Q-ID: 3.6.02
While centrifuging sputum specimens for TB microscopy, a loud crunching sound indicates that a glass tube has shattered inside the running rotor. What is the mandatory immediate action required by Cheesbrough guidelines?
A Immediately pop open the centrifuge lid while the rotor is spinning and spray bleach directly onto the rotor head.
B Switch off the motor immediately and keep the centrifuge lid closed for at least 30 minutes to allow infectious aerosol droplets to settle before opening.
C Increase the speed to maximum to spin the shattered glass out of the buckets.
D Unplug the machine, carry it outside into the sun, and invert it over a trash can.
Option A: Opening the spinning lid releases massive clouds of infectious M. tuberculosis droplet nuclei into the breathing zone of staff.
Option B (CORRECT): The motor must be switched off immediately and the lid kept closed for at least 30 minutes. This allows high-velocity aerosol clouds to settle onto the bowl walls, preventing laboratory-acquired aerosol inhalation. Decontaminate with 10,000 ppm chlorine or 1% Virkon wearing gloves and mask.
Option C: Increasing speed will disintegrate the rotor and launch lethal projectile fragments.
Option D: Inverting disperses infectious debris and ruins the motor shaft alignment.
LEVEL 1 • AUTOCLAVE THERMODYNAMICS Q-ID: 3.6.03
Why is it strictly forbidden to open an autoclave lid immediately after a liquid sterilization cycle when the pressure gauge reaches zero, if the internal temperature is still above 80°C?
A The agar media will permanently solidify into plastic if exposed to cold room air.
B The sudden rush of oxygen will combust the stainless steel autoclave basket.
C Superheated liquids will undergo explosive delayed boiling (boil-over), violently spraying scalding liquid and shattering glass containers onto the operator.
D The pressure gauge will reverse and create an internal vacuum that crushes the chamber.
Option A: Agar remains molten at 80°C and solidifies at ~42°C.
Option B: Stainless steel does not combust with oxygen.
Option C (CORRECT): Liquids inside autoclaves are superheated above their normal boiling point. Releasing the door while liquid is >80°C causes sudden pressure drops and physical disturbance, triggering violent explosive boiling that projects boiling media and shatters glass vessels.
Option D: Vacuum valves prevent chamber crushing.
LEVEL 1 • GLASSWARE REPAIR & flame-smoothing Q-ID: 3.6.04
What is the purpose and correct procedure for "flame-smoothing" chipped glass pipettes and test tubes before reuse in district laboratories?
A Coating the glass in kerosene and lighting it to sterilize spores.
B Rotating the chipped glass rim or tip in the outer blue cone of a Bunsen flame for a few seconds to melt sharp razor edges smooth, preventing finger cuts and rubber bulb damage.
C Holding the glass in the yellow luminous flame until the entire tube collapses shut.
D Dipping red-hot glass into ice water to temper the crystal structure.
Option A: Kerosene is a flammable hazard and ruins glassware.
Option B (CORRECT): flame-smoothing involves rotating the damaged glass edge in the hot non-luminous blue Bunsen flame for 5–10 seconds. The sharp microscopic glass shards melt into a rounded, smooth rim without sealing the orifice, eliminating cut hazards and rubber bulb punctures.
Option C: Collapsing the tube destroys the instrument.
Option D: Dipping hot glass in ice water causes thermal shock explosion.
LEVEL 2 • CENTRIFUGE VIBRATION & MECHANICAL FAILURE Q-ID: 3.6.05
A laboratory technician loads a 15 mL glass tube containing 10 mL of urine on one side of a benchtop centrifuge and balances it with a tube containing 5 mL of water on the opposite side. Upon reaching 3,000 RPM, the centrifuge begins vibrating violently, screeching, and walking across the bench. What fundamental engineering failure occurred?
A Dynamic mass imbalance: opposing centrifuge buckets must be balanced by weight (±0.1 g); unequal volume created severe centrifugal force asymmetry that damaged the rotor spindle.
B Urine has a higher electrical conductivity than water, short-circuiting the rotor brushes.
C The centrifuge was placed on a wooden bench instead of a magnetized iron plate.
D The speed of 3,000 RPM is too slow, causing centrifugal stalling.
Option A (CORRECT): Centrifugal force is proportional to mass ($F = m \cdot \omega^2 \cdot r$). An imbalance of 5 mL (~5 grams) creates hundreds of Newtons of asymmetric lateral force at 3,000 RPM, producing violent mechanical vibration that ruins motor bearings and risks catastrophic rotor disintegration.
Option B: Electrical conductivity inside tubes has no effect on motor brushes.
Option C: Centrifuges require level, sturdy benches, not magnetic plates.
Option D: 3,000 RPM is a standard routine clinical spinning speed.
LEVEL 2 • ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD & FIRE HAZARDS Q-ID: 3.6.06
To power an autoclave (2000W), a water bath (1500W), a centrifuge (500W), and a microscope (50W) simultaneously, a laboratory worker plugs three multi-socket plastic adaptors in series into a single 13A wall outlet. Within 20 minutes, smoke and burning plastic odors emerge from the wall socket. What electrical hazard developed?
A The microscope drew too much current, causing ground leakage.
B Total power exceeded 4,000W (~18A at 220V), massively overloading the 13A rated outlet and multi-adaptors, producing severe $I^2R$ resistive heating and insulation ignition.
C The water bath evaporated the electricity from the wires.
D The autoclave steam polarized the alternating current into high-voltage direct current.
Option A: Microscopes draw minimal current (~0.2A).
Option B (CORRECT): Daisy-chaining high-wattage heating appliances (autoclave + water bath = 3,500W) draws ~18 Amps through a single 13A socket. The excessive current causes extreme $I^2R$ heating across plug pin contacts, melting plastic adaptors and sparking electrical wall fires. Heavy heating equipment must have dedicated high-amperage outlets.
Option C: Electricity does not evaporate.
Option D: Steam does not convert AC to DC in wall wiring.
LEVEL 2 • AUTOCLAVE PRESSURE EQUALIZATION Q-ID: 3.6.07
When preparing 500 mL glass reagent bottles of nutrient broth for autoclaving at 121°C for 15 minutes, what is the mandatory bottle cap adjustment required to prevent container explosion?
A Screw the screw cap down as tightly as possible using a wrench to keep steam out.
B Loosen the screw cap by a half to one full turn (or use breathable foam plugs/foil covers) to allow steam penetration and internal pressure equalization.
C Seal the cap with waterproof electrical tape and superglue.
D Fill the bottle completely to the brim with broth so no air space remains.
Option A: Tight caps trap expanding steam inside the bottle during heating and create a vacuum during cooling, causing explosive glass shattering inside the chamber.
Option B (CORRECT): Caps must be loosened by at least half a turn to allow steam to enter, displace air, and equalize pressure during heating and decompression cycles. Caps are re-tightened only after the autoclave cools and containers are removed.
Option C: Glue and tape melt and create violent overpressure bombs.
Option D: Liquid thermal expansion requires at least 20% headspace; full bottles overflow and burst.
LEVEL 2 • VOLUMETRIC GLASSWARE METROLOGY Q-ID: 3.6.08
A technician uses a calibrated 1-liter Class A volumetric flask to dissolve chemicals by heating the flask directly over a roaring Bunsen burner flame. Why is this practice strictly forbidden in medical laboratory practice?
A Direct flame turns borosilicate glass into opaque radioactive lead.
B Volumetric flasks have thick flat bases that experience severe uneven thermal expansion, leading to sudden thermal fracture explosions and permanent loss of volumetric calibration accuracy.
C The Bunsen flame neutralizes all chemical solutes into nitrogen gas.
D Class A glassware can only be heated in a microwave oven.
Option A: Borosilicate does not turn radioactive.
Option B (CORRECT): Volumetric flasks are precision metrology instruments with thick, flat bases calibrated strictly at 20°C. Direct heating causes uneven expansion stresses that shatter the base and permanently alters the internal volumetric capacity, ruining calibration integrity. Dissolve solids in round-bottom boiling flasks or beakers before transferring.
Option C: Flame heating does not convert solutes to nitrogen.
Option D: Microwaving volumetric flasks is also unsafe for calibration.
Master Overview › Chapter 3: Health and Safety › 3.7 Fire Safety & Emergency First Aid
PART 1 • CHAPTER 3 • SUBUNIT 3.7

Fire Prevention, Extinguisher Classes, Chemical Burn Management & Emergency Resuscitation

Book Pages: 90–93
Section 3.7 Core Examination & Clinical Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 90–93)

Fire Extinguisher Selection & Fire Blankets

Dry Powder & Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) extinguishers are standard for electrical and flammable liquid fires. Never use water on chemical solvent or electrical fires. Woven fiberglass fire blankets are mandatory for smothering clothing flames.

Chemical Splashes: The 15-Minute Rule

For chemical splashes into eyes or on skin, immediate continuous irrigation with cold running water for at least 15 minutes is mandatory (Eye Irrigation Law). Hold eyelids wide open. Never use chemical neutralizing solutions in the eyes.

Electrocution Rescue Protocol

Never touch an electrocuted victim with bare hands while they remain in contact with live current. Isolate mains electricity first, or use a dry non-conductive insulator (wooden stool, dry coat, folded newspaper) to wrench the cable free.

Emergency CPR & Swallowed Poisons

Brain tissue suffers permanent anoxic death after 4 minutes of respiratory arrest. Initiate CPR (30 chest compressions : 2 rescue breaths) immediately. For swallowed strong acids or alkalis: NEVER induce vomiting (causes second-pass esophageal perforation); dilute with water or milk.

1. Laboratory Fire Hazards, Extinguisher Classification & Fire Blankets

According to Cheesbrough (p. 90), chemical solvents, electrical overloads, gas burners, and open flames represent primary ignition risks in district laboratories.

Fire Classification Fuel / Combustible Material Standard Extinguishing Agent Dangerous / Prohibited Actions
Class A Fires Solid organic combustibles (paper archives, wooden benches, cotton overalls). Water spray, foam, or dry chemical powder. Do not use water if energized electrical wiring is in contact.
Class B Fires Flammable liquids and volatile solvents (Ether, Acetone, Methanol, Xylene, Ethanol). Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$), Dry Chemical Powder, or AFFF foam. NEVER USE WATER: Water sinks beneath organic solvents, causing burning liquid to boil, spatter, and spread across the room.
Class C Fires Live energized electrical equipment (Centrifuges, incubators, switchboards, wiring). Dry Powder or Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) extinguishers. NEVER USE WATER OR FOAM: Conducts high-voltage current directly back to the operator, causing fatal electrocution.
Clothing Fires Laboratory protective clothing or personal garments ignited by open Bunsen flame. Woven Fiberglass Fire Blanket: Wrap victim tightly from neck down and roll on floor to smother oxygen. Never allow victim to run (fans flames). Never spray halogenated chemical extinguishers directly onto human faces.

2. Emergency Decontamination: Chemical Splashes, Eye Irrigation & Acid/Alkali Burns

  • Eye Irrigation Protocol: If concentrated acids, caustic alkalis, or formalin splash into the eyes, guide the victim to the emergency eye-wash station immediately. Irrigate the eye continuously with clean, gentle running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the upper and lower eyelids wide open to wash out the conjunctival sacs. Never instill neutralizing acid or alkali solutions into the eye. Cover with sterile pad and refer to ophthalmologist immediately.
  • Extensive Skin Chemical Burns: Remove contaminated clothing immediately under an emergency safety shower or running tap. Flush affected skin with abundant cold water for 15–20 minutes. For acid burns, apply a cold compress of sodium bicarbonate solution; for caustic alkali burns, apply dilute vinegar (5% acetic acid).
  • Thermal Burns & Scalds: Immerse the burned area immediately in cold water or apply clean wet cloths for 10 minutes until pain subsides. Cover loosely with sterile dry dressing. Never apply butter, grease, or adhesive tape to burns.

3. First Aid Protocols for Swallowed Poisons & Inhaled Toxic Gases

Ingested / Inhaled Substance Immediate Life-Saving First Aid Action Strict Prohibitions & Medical Warnings
Concentrated Mineral Acids ($HCl, H_2SO_4, HNO_3$) Immediately give water or milk to drink (1–2 cups) to dilute the acid in the stomach. Give milk of magnesia if available. NEVER INDUCE VOMITING: Regurgitating strong acid burns the esophagus, pharynx, and mouth a second time, causing fatal perforation.
Caustic Alkalis ($NaOH, KOH$, Conc. Ammonia) Give water or milk immediately to dilute. Give sips of diluted vinegar or lemon juice. NEVER INDUCE VOMITING: Caustic liquefaction necrosis severely damages esophageal tissues.
Potassium Cyanide ($KCN$) Break an Amyl Nitrite ampoule in a clean cloth and hold under victim's nose for 15 seconds every minute. Give oxygen. Transfer immediately to hospital for IV Sodium Nitrite & Sodium Thiosulfate antidote. Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen respiration. Immediate action within 1–2 minutes is critical to prevent fatal cardiac arrest.
Toxic Inhaled Gases ($Cl_2, HCN, NO_2, NH_3$) Remove victim immediately into fresh air. Loosen tight collar and belt. Keep warm and quiet in recovery position. Administer oxygen if trained. Rescuer must wear self-contained respiratory mask before entering gas-filled room.

4. Electrocution Rescue, Recovery Position & Emergency CPR

  • Electrocution Rescue Sequence:
    1. Do not touch the victim's body with bare hands while they are in contact with the live current.
    2. Switch off the electrical current at the main switchboard or pull the plug.
    3. If the switch cannot be reached, stand on a dry wooden board or rubber mat, wrap hands in thick dry cloth or newspaper, and use a dry wooden broomstick or chair to wrench the victim free from the live wire.
  • The Recovery Position: For an unconscious breathing patient (e.g. following severe fainting or electric shock), place the victim on their side with the chin tilted up, head turned to one side (to prevent tongue obstruction and aspiration of vomitus), upper arm bent at 90°, and upper leg flexed at hip and knee.
  • Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR):
    • Check responsiveness and feel for carotid pulse in the neck groove for 5–10 seconds.
    • If pulse and breathing are absent, place the heel of one hand over the lower half of the sternum (breastbone) with the other hand interlocked on top.
    • Deliver 30 rapid chest compressions (depth 5 cm, rate 100–120/min) followed by 2 effective rescue breaths (tilt head, pinch nose, blow until chest visibly rises). Continue the 30:2 cycle until medical help arrives.
Section 3.7 Interactive Board Examination (8 MCQs)
LEVEL 1 • FIRE EXTINGUISHER SELECTION Q-ID: 3.7.01
Which type of fire extinguisher is specifically recommended by Cheesbrough (p. 90) for extinguishing fires involving flammable organic solvents (ether, xylene) and energized electrical equipment in district laboratories?
A High-pressure water hose.
B Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) or Dry Chemical Powder extinguisher.
C Aqueous detergent solution.
D Concentrated hydrochloric acid spray.
Option A: Water spreads burning organic solvents and conducts high-voltage current to the user.
Option B (CORRECT): Dry Chemical Powder and Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) extinguishers smother flames by displacing oxygen and interrupting chemical flame propagation without conducting electricity, making them safe for Class B (solvents) and Class C (electrical) laboratory fires.
Option C: Detergents contain water and conduct electrical currents.
Option D: Acid releases corrosive, suffocating fumes and intensifies fires.
LEVEL 1 • CHEMICAL EYE DECONTAMINATION Q-ID: 3.7.02
If concentrated acid or caustic sodium hydroxide solution accidentally splashes into a laboratory worker's eyes, what is the mandatory immediate first aid response?
A Instill concentrated hydrochloric acid into the eye to neutralize alkaline burns.
B Irrigate the eye immediately and continuously with clean, gentle running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids wide open.
C Rub the eyes vigorously with dry gauze and apply petroleum jelly.
D Keep the eyes tightly closed and wait 2 hours for natural tears to wash the chemical away.
Option A: Instilling neutralizing chemicals into eyes causes severe thermal and chemical injury.
Option B (CORRECT): Continuous irrigation with clean running water for at least 15 minutes with eyelids retracted is the universally mandated first aid procedure. It rapidly dilutes and washes out corrosive chemicals before permanent corneal ulceration or blindness occurs.
Option C: Rubbing scratches the cornea with glass or chemical crystals.
Option D: Keeping eyes closed traps corrosive caustic chemicals against the cornea, leading to total blindness.
LEVEL 1 • SWALLOWED POISON MANAGEMENT Q-ID: 3.7.03
Why is the induction of vomiting strictly contraindicated when a patient has accidentally swallowed concentrated hydrochloric acid or caustic potassium hydroxide?
A Vomiting converts corrosive acids into explosive nitroglycerin inside the throat.
B Regurgitating corrosive substances causes secondary severe chemical burns and perforation to the esophagus, pharynx, and vocal cords, alongside catastrophic pulmonary aspiration.
C Corrosive acids are neutralized by stomach bile within 5 minutes.
D Vomiting causes the patient's blood group to change.
Option A: Acids do not synthesize nitroglycerin in vivo.
Option B (CORRECT): Inducing vomiting forces corrosive chemicals back up the already damaged esophagus and throat, causing transmural esophageal perforation, mediastinitis, vocal cord destruction, and fatal chemical pneumonitis if aspirated. Immediate dilution with water or milk is the correct protocol.
Option C: Concentrated acids overpower stomach buffering and cause severe gastric necrosis.
Option D: Blood group antigens are unaffected by chemical ingestion.
LEVEL 1 • ELECTROCUTION RESCUE SAFETY Q-ID: 3.7.04
A laboratory worker is seen convulsing while holding a live 240V centrifuge cable with the power switch out of reach. What must a rescuer do before attempting to touch the victim?
A Grab the victim's bare wrists with both hands and pull backwards forcefully.
B Stand on a dry non-conductive surface (wood, rubber mat), wrap hands in dry thick cloth or newspaper, and use a dry wooden stick to push the victim or cable free.
C Throw a bucket of water over the victim to cool the electrical wire.
D Touch the victim's feet with a metal steel rod.
Option A: Touching the victim's bare skin with bare hands conducts the 240V current through the rescuer's body, causing dual electrocution.
Option B (CORRECT): Rescuers must strictly insulate themselves from the ground and the victim using dry non-conductive materials (dry wood, rubber, folded cloth, newspaper) to break electrical contact safely without becoming a victim.
Option C: Water conducts electricity across the entire floor, electrocuting everyone present.
Option D: Metal conducts live current directly into the rescuer's hands.
LEVEL 2 • CARDIOPULMONARY RESUSCITATION PROTOCOLS Q-ID: 3.7.05
Following a severe electric shock, a laboratory worker is unconscious, non-responsive, with absent breathing and no palpable carotid pulse. What is the standard adult CPR compression-to-ventilation ratio that must be started immediately?
A 30 chest compressions (depth 5 cm, rate 100–120/min) followed by 2 rescue breaths.
B 5 chest compressions followed by 10 rescue breaths.
C 50 rescue breaths with zero chest compressions.
D Continuous rapid slapping of the patient's face for 10 minutes.
Option A (CORRECT): Standard international adult CPR guidelines mandate a continuous cycle of 30 high-quality chest compressions (depth ~5 cm over the lower sternum at 100–120 compressions/min) followed by 2 effective rescue breaths until spontaneous circulation returns or defibrillation is available.
Option B: 5:10 ratio provides inadequate cardiac forward perfusion.
Option C: Without chest compressions, blood cannot circulate to the brain and vital organs.
Option D: Slapping does not treat cardiac arrest and wastes critical resuscitation time.
LEVEL 2 • TOXICOLOGY & CYANIDE EMERGENCY FIRST AID Q-ID: 3.7.06
A technician preparing Drabkin's solution accidentally splashes Potassium Cyanide powder into their mouth and collapses with rapid gasping and convulsions. What is the immediate life-saving first aid antidote that must be administered within 60 seconds?
A Force the victim to drink 1 liter of concentrated vinegar.
B Crush an Amyl Nitrite ampoule in a clean cloth and hold it under the victim's nose for 15 seconds every minute, administer 100% oxygen, and arrange urgent IV sodium nitrite/thiosulfate therapy.
C Induce vomiting by inserting a finger into the throat.
D Give hot black tea with sugar and place victim in direct sunlight.
Option A: Vinegar is acidic and liberates lethal hydrogen cyanide gas in the mouth/stomach.
Option B (CORRECT): Inhaling crushed Amyl Nitrite rapidly generates methemoglobin in the blood ($Fe^{3+}$), which has a higher binding affinity for cyanide than mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, stripping cyanide away from cells until intravenous sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate convert it into harmless thiocyanate.
Option C: Vomiting during cyanide convulsions leads to fatal aspiration.
Option D: Tea has zero antidotal activity against cyanide.
LEVEL 2 • POST-ACCIDENT PATIENT POSITIONING Q-ID: 3.7.07
A laboratory worker faints and loses consciousness following a severe glass laceration. They are breathing normally and have a strong radial pulse. What is the correct posture to place the unconscious victim in while awaiting medical transport?
A The Recovery Position: lying on their side with head tilted back, chin extended downwards, and upper limbs bent to maintain an open airway and prevent aspiration of saliva/vomit.
B Sitting upright in an office chair with the head hanging forward between the knees.
C Lying flat on the back (supine) with a large pillow propping the head high.
D Standing upright supported against a wall.
Option A (CORRECT): The lateral Recovery Position stabilizes the patient on their side, keeping the airway clear by allowing the tongue to fall forward and fluid/vomitus to drain freely out of the mouth, preventing fatal asphyxiation.
Option B: Sitting an unconscious person restricts cerebral blood flow and causes airway collapse.
Option C: Lying supine allows the flaccid tongue to block the posterior pharynx, causing complete airway obstruction.
Option D: Standing is impossible in an unconscious patient and leads to falls.
LEVEL 2 • HEMORRHAGE CONTROL & SHOCK PREVENTION Q-ID: 3.7.08
A large glass Winchester bottle breaks, deeply lacerating a technician's forearm. Bright red blood is spurting rapidly from the wound (pulsatile arterial hemorrhage). What is the mandatory immediate step to prevent fatal hemorrhagic shock?
A Pour alcohol directly into the open wound and allow blood to drain freely to clean the cut.
B Apply firm, direct continuous pressure over the bleeding site using a sterile pad or clean cloth, elevate the injured arm above heart level, and apply a pressure bandage.
C Place the arm in hot water for 30 minutes to dilate blood vessels.
D Give the patient aspirin tablets and leave the wound unbandaged.
Option A: Alcohol causes intense pain and cell lysis; allowing arterial blood to drain leads to fatal hypovolemic shock.
Option B (CORRECT): Direct firm pressure over the bleeding vessel using a sterile dressing combined with limb elevation above the level of the heart reduces hydrostatic pressure and arrests arterial hemorrhage effectively. Never remove blood-soaked pads; add fresh dressings on top and secure firmly.
Option C: Hot water increases vasodilation and accelerates blood loss.
Option D: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent that worsens bleeding.
