    • Cyst: Oval (\(8 ext{–}12 imes 7 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\)), distinct smooth cyst wall, 4 nuclei (usually at one pole), central longitudinal axostyle and curved transverse median/parabasal bodies.
  • Dientamoeba fragilis:
    • Unique Biology: An unflagellated trichomonad flagellate. Exists strictly as a trophozoite (\(5 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)); has no cyst stage.
    • Morphology: 60–80% of trophozoites are binucleated; each nucleus has a characteristic fragmented karyosome consisting of 4–8 chromatin granules. Transmitted in the protective eggs of Enterobius vermicularis pinworms.
  • Trichomonas hominis (Pentatrichomonas hominis):
    • Biology: Non-pathogenic commensal flagellate inhabiting the caecum; strictly trophozoite stage (\(7 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)), no cyst stage.
    • Motility & Structure: Fast, jerky, rotary motility; 5 anterior flagella and an undulating membrane extending the full length of the body with a trailing recurrent flagellum.
  • Chilomastix mesnili:
    • Biology: Non-pathogenic commensal; trophozoite is pear-shaped (\(10 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a spiral body groove and jerky progressive motility.
    • Cyst: Characteristic lemon-shaped / pear-shaped (\(6 ext{–}9\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a prominent anterior nipple-like protuberance and single nucleus with curved cytostomal fibril ("shepherd's crook").
  • Balantidium coli:
    • Epidemiology & Biology: Zoonotic parasite of domestic pigs; largest protozoan infecting humans. Trophozoites invade the large intestine producing deep ulcers resembling amoebic dysentery.
    • Trophozoite: Massive (\(50 ext{–}200 imes 40 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\)), completely covered in longitudinal rows of cilia, anterior funnel-shaped peristome/cytostome, large kidney-shaped macronucleus and small spherical micronucleus.
    • Cyst: Large spherical (\(50 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\)), double-layered refractile wall enclosing macronucleus; cilia visible inside young cysts.

3. Intestinal Coccidia & Microsporidia (Cheesbrough pp. 214–216)

Intestinal coccidia are obligate intracellular protozoa that undergo complex schizogony (asexual) and gametogony (sexual) within enterocytes. Cysts (oocysts) are acid-fast:

Coccidian Organism Oocyst Dimensions & Shape Modified ZN Staining Profile UV Autofluorescence Sporulation State at Excretion
Cryptosporidium parvum / hominis \(4 ext{–}6\ \mu ext{m}\); spherical / subspherical; contains 4 naked sporozoites. Uniformly Acid-Fast: Stains intense bright pinkish-red to deep fuchsia against malachite green/methylene blue background. Non-autofluorescent. Fully sporulated & immediately infective when passed in faeces. Autoinfection occurs via thin-walled oocysts.
Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli) \(20 ext{–}33 imes 10 ext{–}19\ \mu ext{m}\); elongated elliptical / spindle-shaped with tapered neck. Acid-Fast: Stains brilliant red/pink; sporoblasts stain deep magenta. Strong blue/green autofluorescence under \(330 ext{–}380 ext{ nm}\) UV excitation. Unsporulated when excreted; contains 1 single round sporoblast (later divides into 2 sporocysts each with 4 sporozoites).
Cyclospora cayetanensis \(8 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\); spherical; contains central morula-like sphere of refractile globules. Variably Acid-Fast: "Ghost" forms stain faint pink or remain unstained; others stain deep red-purple. Intense blue-green autofluorescence under \(365 ext{ nm}\) UV filter. Unsporulated when excreted; requires 1–2 weeks in environment to sporulate into 2 sporocysts with 2 sporozoites each. Direct person-to-person spread does not occur.
Microsporidia (Enterocytozoon bieneusi / Encephalitozoon intestinalis) \(1.0 ext{–}2.5\ \mu ext{m}\); extremely tiny oval spores with coiled internal polar filament/tube. Modified Trichrome (Weber-Green) or Calcofluor White: Spores stain bright pinkish-red with a distinctive diagonal/horizontal belt strip across the middle. Intense white/blue under Calcofluor UV illumination. Mature infective spores with high environmental resistance.

Section 5.4 Interactive Examination Bank (8 High-Yield Clinical MCQs)

Test your diagnostic competence on amoebic differentiation, cyst chromatoid morphology, flagellate kinematics, and coccidian acid-fast stains:

Question 5.4.1 (Q273): In a patient presenting with acute dysentery, bloody mucoid stools, and severe tenesmus, microscopic examination of a fresh warm saline wet mount reveals active amoebic trophozoites (\(25\ \mu ext{m}\)). What single morphological finding provides absolute, pathognomonic confirmation of invasive Entamoeba histolytica, definitively ruling out the commensal Entamoeba dispar?
Correct Answer: B (Erythrophagocytosis / Ingested Red Blood Cells)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 208–210 & Plate 5.4: Under light microscopy, Entamoeba histolytica and the non-pathogenic commensal Entamoeba dispar are completely identical in size, nuclear structure (pinpoint central karyosome, regular peripheral chromatin), and cyst morphology. The only microscopic feature that definitively establishes invasive E. histolytica disease is the presence of phagocytosed red blood cells within the cytoplasm of actively motile trophozoites. Cysts never ingest RBCs.
Question 5.4.2 (Q274): A stool iodine preparation reveals spherical cysts measuring \(18\ \mu ext{m}\) in diameter containing 8 distinct nuclei with eccentric karyosomes, and occasional ragged, splinter-like chromatoid bodies with sharp pointed ends. What is the correct identification of this organism?
Correct Answer: C (Entamoeba coli)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 210–211: Mature cysts of Entamoeba coli measure \(15 ext{–}30\ \mu ext{m}\) and typically contain 8 nuclei (occasionally 16) with coarse, irregular peripheral chromatin and an eccentric karyosome. The chromatoid bodies of E. coli are characteristically splinter-like with sharp, fractured, pointed ends. In contrast, E. histolytica cysts have at most 4 nuclei and smooth, rounded, cigar-shaped chromatoid bars.
Question 5.4.3 (Q275): A patient with chronic fatty diarrhoea (steatorrhoea), abdominal bloating, and flatulence provides a fresh stool sample. Microscopic saline wet mount demonstrates actively motile pear-shaped trophozoites that tumble and roll across the field with a characteristic "falling-leaf" motion. What organism is responsible?
Correct Answer: A (Giardia lamblia)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 211–213 & Plate 5.6: Giardia lamblia trophozoites are pear-shaped (\(10 ext{–}18\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a concave ventral sucking disc, 2 anterior nuclei resembling eyeglasses ("old man appearance"), and 4 pairs of flagella that propel the parasite in a slow, fluttering, tumbling falling-leaf motility. It adheres to duodenal enterocytes, causing non-invasive malabsorptive steatorrhoea.
Question 5.4.4 (Q276): Which of the following intestinal flagellates exists exclusively in the trophozoite stage with no recognized cyst form in its life cycle, is predominantly binucleated with fragmented karyosomes, and is transmitted via the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis?
Correct Answer: D (Dientamoeba fragilis)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 213: Dientamoeba fragilis is an amoeboflagellate related to trichomonads that lacks flagella and has no cyst stage. 60–80% of trophozoites possess 2 nuclei, each containing 4–8 distinct chromatin granules. Because the naked trophozoite is fragile in the external environment, it relies on vector transport inside the eggs of the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis for transmission.
Question 5.4.5 (Q277): An advanced HIV/AIDS patient (\( ext{CD4} = 65/\mu ext{L}\)) develops chronic intractable watery diarrhoea (15 bowel movements/day). A modified Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain of the faecal concentrate reveals numerous small, round, intensely acid-fast oocysts measuring \(4 ext{–}6\ \mu ext{m}\) in diameter staining bright magenta-red. What is the diagnosis?
Correct Answer: B (Cryptosporidium parvum / hominis)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 214–216 & Plate 5.11: Cryptosporidium oocysts measure \(4 ext{–}6\ \mu ext{m}\) and are uniformly acid-fast, staining bright pink-red on modified ZN. Cyclospora oocysts are larger (\(8 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\)) and show variable acid-fastness. Cystoisospora oocysts are much larger (\(20 ext{–}33\ \mu ext{m}\)) and spindle-shaped. In immunocompromised patients, Cryptosporidium causes life-threatening secretory cholera-like enteritis.
Question 5.4.6 (Q278): A stool specimen examined under ultraviolet microscopy (\(365 ext{ nm}\) excitation) reveals spherical, unsporulated coccidian oocysts measuring \(8 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\) in diameter that exhibit intense, brilliant blue-green autofluorescence. On modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining, some oocysts stain dark red while others appear as unstained "ghosts". What parasite is this?
Correct Answer: C (Cyclospora cayetanensis)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 216 & Plate 5.12: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts are spherical, measure \(8 ext{–}10\ \mu ext{m}\) (twice the diameter of Cryptosporidium), display variable acid-fastness ("ghost forms" vs red stained forms), and exhibit intense blue-green autofluorescence under UV epifluorescence. They are unsporulated when passed and require 1–2 weeks in the environment to mature.
Question 5.4.7 (Q279): A farmer from a rural swine-raising region presents with severe dysentery, colonic ulceration, and bloody diarrhoea. Wet mount examination reveals massive, rapidly swimming ciliated protozoan trophozoites (\(120\ \mu ext{m}\) long) containing a conspicuous, large, kidney-shaped macronucleus. What is the organism?
Correct Answer: A (Balantidium coli)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 213 & Plate 5.8: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan and the only ciliate known to infect humans. Pigs serve as the principal domestic reservoir. Trophozoites measure \(50 ext{–}200\ \mu ext{m}\), are covered in cilia, possess an anterior cytostome and a distinct kidney-shaped / bean-shaped macronucleus, and burrow into the colonic mucosa causing severe balantidial dysentery.
Question 5.4.8 (Q280): Stool examination of an asymptomatic individual reveals small, non-motile, lemon-shaped cysts measuring \(7\ \mu ext{m}\) with a distinctive anterior nipple-like protrusion and a single nucleus adjacent to a curved cytostomal fibril resembling a shepherd's crook. What is this non-pathogenic commensal?
Correct Answer: D (Chilomastix mesnili)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 213: Cysts of the non-pathogenic flagellate Chilomastix mesnili are unmistakable due to their characteristic lemon-shaped / pear-shaped morphology (\(6 ext{–}9\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a distinct anterior knob or nipple. Internally, a single nucleus and a prominent curved cytostomal cleft/fibril (the "shepherd's crook") are visible. Recognition prevents unnecessary treatment.
Master Overview › Chapter 5: Parasitological Tests › 5.5 Identification of Helminth Eggs & Larvae
PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.5

Identification of Helminth Eggs & Larvae: Nematodes, Hookworms, Strongyloides & Intestinal Schistosomes

Book Pages: 216–227
Section 5.5 Core Examination & Clinical Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 216–227)

1. Soil-Transmitted Nematode Triad

• Ascaris lumbricoides: Fertile egg (\(45 ext{–}75 imes 35 ext{–}50\ \mu ext{m}\)) with thick brown mamillated albuminous coat; infertile egg (\(85 ext{–}95\ \mu ext{m}\)) elongated with irregular yolk granules.
• Trichuris trichiura: Barrel-shaped (\(50 ext{–}55 imes 22 ext{–}24\ \mu ext{m}\)) with prominent transparent bipolar mucoid plugs; causes rectal prolapse.
• Hookworms: Oval, thin transparent shell (\(60 imes 40\ \mu ext{m}\)) containing a 4–8 cell morula.

2. The Hookworm vs Strongyloides Rule

In fresh faeces, hookworms pass eggs, while Strongyloides stercoralis passes living rhabditiform larvae (\( ext{L}_1\)).
• Strongyloides \( ext{L}_1\): Short buccal cavity (\(4\ \mu ext{m}\)) + large prominent genital primordium.
• Hookworm \( ext{L}_1\): Long buccal cavity (\(15\ \mu ext{m}\)) + inconspicuous genital primordium.

3. Strongyloides Hyperinfection Syndrome

S. stercoralis is capable of internal autoinfection. In patients on corticosteroids or co-infected with HTLV-1 / HIV, uncontrolled larval multiplication causes hyperinfection syndrome & disseminated strongyloidiasis with fatal Gram-negative bacterial sepsis and meningitis.

4. Intestinal Schistosome Spine Diagnostics

• Schistosoma mansoni: Large egg (\(114 ext{–}180 imes 45 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a prominent, sharp lateral spine.
• Schistosoma japonicum: Subspherical egg (\(70 ext{–}100 imes 50 ext{–}65\ \mu ext{m}\)) with an inconspicuous small lateral knob/spine.
• Schistosoma intercalatum: Elongated egg (\(140 ext{–}240 imes 50 ext{–}85\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a long terminal spine (Ziehl-Neelsen positive / acid-fast shell).

1. Intestinal Nematodes (Soil-Transmitted Helminths) (Cheesbrough pp. 216–224)

Soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) infect over 1.5 billion people worldwide. Transmission occurs through ingestion of infective eggs or transcutaneous larval penetration:

  • Ascaris lumbricoides (Giant Intestinal Roundworm):
    • Adult Worm: Cylindrical, tapered ends; creamy-white or pinkish. Males measure \(15 ext{–}30 ext{ cm}\) with a curved posterior tail and two copulatory spicules; females measure \(20 ext{–}35 ext{ cm}\) (up to \(40 ext{ cm}\)). Inhabit the lumen of the small intestine (jejunum).
    • Clinical Pathology: Larval pulmonary migration causes Loeffler's syndrome (dry cough, wheezing, transient pulmonary infiltrates, and marked peripheral eosinophilia). Adult worm boluses cause mechanical intestinal obstruction, volvulus, intussusception, wandering into the biliary duct (obstructive jaundice/cholangitis) or pancreatic duct (acute pancreatitis).
    • Fertile Eggs: Round/oval (\(45 ext{–}75 imes 35 ext{–}50\ \mu ext{m}\)); golden-brown bile-stained, thick multi-layered shell covered with an external coarse, rough, tubercular mamillated albuminous coat enclosing an unsegmented single-celled ovum. Decorticated eggs lack the outer albumin layer.
    • Infertile Eggs: Passed by unfertilized females; larger, narrower, and more elongated (\(85 ext{–}95 imes 40 ext{–}45\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a thinner shell and disorganized irregular mamillations completely filled with refractile yolk granules.
  • Trichuris trichiura (Whipworm):
    • Morphology: Adult worm measures \(3 ext{–}5 ext{ cm}\); anterior three-fifths is extremely attenuated and thread-like (whip), while posterior two-fifths is thick and stout (handle). Thread-like anterior end is threaded into the mucosa of the caecum and ascending colon.
    • Clinical Pathology: Heavy chronic infection in malnourished children leads to Trichuris Dysentery Syndrome (TDS): chronic mucoid bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus, severe microcytic anaemia, finger clubbing, growth retardation, and rectal prolapse due to tenesmus and colonic wall friability.
    • Diagnostic Egg: Distinctive barrel-shaped / football-shaped (\(50 ext{–}55 imes 22 ext{–}24\ \mu ext{m}\)), thick smooth golden-yellowish-brown shell with prominent, transparent bipolar mucoid plugs (prominences) at both ends. Contains an unsegmented ovum.
  • Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale & Necator americanus):
    • Species Comparison:
      • Ancylostoma duodenale (Old World Hookworm): Buccal capsule has two pairs of sharp curved ventral teeth. Larger (\(8 ext{–}13 ext{ mm}\)); blood loss per worm = \(0.20 ext{ mL/day}\) (10 times more virulent).
      • Necator americanus (New World Hookworm): Buccal capsule has one pair of ventral semi-lunar cutting plates and one pair of dorsal plates. Smaller (\(5 ext{–}11 ext{ mm}\)); blood loss per worm = \(0.03 ext{ mL/day}\).
    • Clinical Pathology: Skin penetration causes intense pruritic dermatitis ("Ground Itch"); pulmonary larval migration causes mild pneumonitis; chronic blood sucking leads to insidious, severe microcytic hypochromic iron deficiency anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia with peripheral oedema.
    • Diagnostic Egg: Oval, blunt rounded poles (\(55 ext{–}75 imes 35 ext{–}40\ \mu ext{m}\)); extremely thin, transparent, colourless single shell containing a central segmented ovum (typically 4 to 8 blastomeres) separated from the shell by a distinct clear halo space.

2. Strongyloides stercoralis & Hookworm Larval Differentiation (Cheesbrough pp. 221–224)

Strongyloides stercoralis (threadworm) is unique among helminths because it can complete its entire life cycle either in free-living soil or inside the human host via autoinfection:

Diagnostic Feature Strongyloides stercoralis Larva Hookworm (Ancylostoma / Necator) Larva
Stage in Fresh Faeces First-stage Rhabditiform Larva (\( ext{L}_1\)) (Eggs hatch in the intestinal mucosa). Eggs containing 4–8 cells (Larvae only appear if stool is left standing at room temperature for \(>24 ext{ hours}\)).
Buccal Cavity (\( ext{L}_1\)) Very Short (\(3 ext{–}5\ \mu ext{m}\)), shorter than the width of the larval head. Long (\(12 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)), equal to or longer than the width of the larval head.
Genital Primordium (\( ext{L}_1\)) Large, conspicuous, prominent hourglass-shaped mass of cells in the posterior third. Small, inconspicuous, dot-like, difficult to visualize.
Third-Stage Filariform Larva (\( ext{L}_3\)) Long filariform esophagus (occupies half of body length); tail tip is notched / bifid / forked. Short esophagus (occupies one-third of body length); tail tip is sharply pointed.

3. Intestinal Schistosomes (Blood Flukes) (Cheesbrough pp. 224–227)

Schistosomes are dioecious (separate sexes) digenetic trematodes that reside within the mesenteric and pelvic venules of the human vascular system:

Schistosoma Species Egg Dimensions & Spine Architecture Snail Intermediate Host Adult Venous Habitat & Clinical Pathology
Schistosoma mansoni \(114 ext{–}180 imes 45 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\); yellowish-brown; prominent, sharp, curved lateral spine near posterior pole. Contains living ciliated miracidium. Aquatic planorbid snails: Biomphalaria spp. (B. pfeifferi, B. alexandrina, B. glabrata). Inferior mesenteric venules of colon. Causes intestinal bilharziasis (bloody diarrhoea, polyps) and granulomatous Symmers' pipestem periportal hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension and esophageal varices.
Schistosoma japonicum \(70 ext{–}100 imes 50 ext{–}65\ \mu ext{m}\); rounded/subspherical; small, inconspicuous rudimentary lateral knob / spine in a shallow depression. Amphibious operculate snails: Oncomelania spp. (O. hupensis). Superior and inferior mesenteric venules draining small & large intestine. Produces severe Katayama fever, extensive hepatic fibrosis, and ectopic brain embolization with seizures.
Schistosoma intercalatum \(140 ext{–}240 imes 50 ext{–}85\ \mu ext{m}\); elongated spindle-shaped; long, sharp terminal spine (often with a slight equatorial curve). Acid-fast shell: Stains bright red with Ziehl-Neelsen stain. Freshwater bulinid snails: Bulinus spp. (B. forskalii group). Mesenteric plexus draining the rectum. Causes localized rectal schistosomiasis in West and Central Africa.
Schistosoma mekongi \(50 ext{–}65 imes 40 ext{–}55\ \mu ext{m}\); smaller, spherical; tiny lateral knob (Mekong River basin). Freshwater snail: Neotricula aperta. Mesenteric venules in Cambodia and Laos.

Section 5.5 Interactive Examination Bank (8 High-Yield Clinical MCQs)

Test your diagnostic competence on egg morphology, larval differential anatomy, life cycles, and clinical helminthology:

Question 5.5.1 (Q281): Examination of a fresh stool specimen from a patient with profound iron deficiency anaemia reveals oval, colourless, thin-shelled eggs measuring \(65 imes 38\ \mu ext{m}\) with a clear space between the shell and an internal 8-cell morula. Stool culture via the Harada-Mori method produces third-stage filariform larvae with a short esophagus and a sharply pointed tail tip. What organism is confirmed?
Correct Answer: B (Hookworm: Ancylostoma duodenale / Necator americanus)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 220–221: Hookworm eggs are characteristically thin-shelled, transparent, oval, and passed in the 4–8 cell morula stage. The infective third-stage filariform larva (\( ext{L}_3\)) of hookworms is distinguished by a short esophagus (occupying one-third of the body length) and a sharply pointed tail tip, whereas Strongyloides filariform larvae have a long esophagus (half body length) and a notched / bifid tail tip.
Question 5.5.2 (Q282): A laboratory technician examines a fresh diarrhoeic stool specimen immediately after collection and observes actively moving rhabditiform larvae (\( ext{L}_1\)) measuring \(250\ \mu ext{m}\). Microscopic measurement under \(40 imes\) magnification reveals a very short buccal cavity (\(4\ \mu ext{m}\)) and a large, prominent hourglass-shaped genital primordium in the mid-body. What is the identity of this parasite?
Correct Answer: A (Strongyloides stercoralis)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 223 & Plate 5.18/5.19: Strongyloides stercoralis is the only human intestinal nematode whose eggs hatch inside the intestinal mucosa, resulting in the passage of living first-stage rhabditiform larvae (\( ext{L}_1\)) in fresh faeces. The diagnostic features are a short buccal cavity (\(3 ext{–}5\ \mu ext{m}\), shorter than head width) and a conspicuous, large genital primordium. In contrast, hookworm \( ext{L}_1\) larvae (which only hatch in aged stool) have a long buccal cavity (\(12 ext{–}15\ \mu ext{m}\)) and an inconspicuous genital primordium.
Question 5.5.3 (Q283): A 5-year-old child presenting with severe chronic dysentery, growth failure, microcytic anaemia, and rectal prolapse has stool microscopy showing characteristic barrel-shaped golden-brown eggs (\(52 imes 23\ \mu ext{m}\)) with prominent transparent bipolar mucoid plugs. What is the causative organism?
Correct Answer: C (Trichuris trichiura)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 219–220 & Plate 5.14: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) produces unmistakable golden-brown, barrel-shaped eggs with distinct transparent bipolar mucoid prominences / plugs. In heavy paediatric infections (Trichuris dysentery syndrome), thousands of worms embedded in the friable colonic mucosa produce chronic tenesmus, bloody diarrhoea, and hallmark rectal prolapse.
Question 5.5.4 (Q284): Stool examination of a patient from an endemic area in East Africa with hepatosplenomegaly and rectal bleeding reveals large, elongated, yellowish-brown eggs measuring \(150 imes 60\ \mu ext{m}\) that possess a prominent, sharp, curved lateral spine near the posterior pole. What species is this?
Correct Answer: B (Schistosoma mansoni)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 224–226 & Plate 5.21: Schistosoma mansoni eggs measure \(114 ext{–}180 imes 45 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\) and are definitively characterized by a large, sharp, triangular lateral spine. They are excreted in faeces from adult worms inhabiting the inferior mesenteric venules. S. haematobium and S. intercalatum possess terminal spines, whereas S. japonicum has an inconspicuous lateral knob.
Question 5.5.5 (Q285): A patient on high-dose immunosuppressive corticosteroid therapy for systemic lupus erythematosus suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, paralytic ileus, diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and polymicrobial Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteraemia with meningitis. What parasitic complication must be immediately suspected?
Correct Answer: D (Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 222: When cell-mediated immunity is suppressed by corticosteroids or HTLV-1 infection, Strongyloides autoinfection escalates uncontrollably. Millions of filariform larvae penetrate the bowel wall and migrate throughout the lungs, liver, and central nervous system. Migrating larvae breach the intestinal mucosal barrier and carry enteric bacteria into the bloodstream, triggering recurrent Gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis with high mortality.
Question 5.5.6 (Q286): Which of the following snail species serves as the obligatory intermediate host for the transmission of Schistosoma mansoni in tropical Africa, the Middle East, and South America?
Correct Answer: A (Biomphalaria species)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 225: Biomphalaria planorbid aquatic snails are the specific intermediate hosts for Schistosoma mansoni. Bulinus snails transmit S. haematobium and S. intercalatum; Oncomelania transmits S. japonicum; and Lymnaea snails transmit Fasciola hepatica and F. gigantica.
Question 5.5.7 (Q287): What key anatomical feature distinguishes the adult buccal capsule of Ancylostoma duodenale from that of Necator americanus, explaining its higher blood consumption rate (\(0.20 ext{ mL/worm/day}\) vs \(0.03 ext{ mL/worm/day}\))?
Correct Answer: B (Ancylostoma has two pairs of curved ventral teeth; Necator has cutting plates)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 220: The buccal capsule of Ancylostoma duodenale is equipped with two pairs of large, sharp curved teeth on the ventral margin, allowing deep, lacerating bites into mucosal villi that extract \(0.14 ext{–}0.20 ext{ mL}\) of blood per day. Necator americanus possesses a pair of blunt semi-lunar cutting plates, resulting in less tissue trauma and a lower blood loss of \(0.02 ext{–}0.05 ext{ mL}\) per worm per day.
Question 5.5.8 (Q288): A stool sample from Central Africa contains large, elongated eggs (\(180 imes 65\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a sharp terminal spine. How can a medical laboratory technologist definitively differentiate Schistosoma intercalatum eggs from ectopic Schistosoma haematobium eggs in stool?
Correct Answer: C (Ziehl-Neelsen staining: S. intercalatum is acid-fast positive; S. haematobium is negative)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 227 & Plate 5.22: Both S. intercalatum and S. haematobium possess terminal spines. However, the egg shell of S. intercalatum is strongly acid-fast positive, retaining carbol fuchsin and staining bright crimson-red in the modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain. In contrast, the egg shell of S. haematobium is completely acid-fast negative (decolorizes and takes up the blue/green counterstain).
Master Overview › Chapter 5: Parasitological Tests › 5.6 Flukes, Tapeworms & Enterobius
PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.6

Identification of Trematodes (Flukes), Cestodes (Tapeworms) & Enterobius vermicularis

Book Pages: 227–243
Section 5.6 Core Examination & Clinical Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 227–243)

1. The Taenia Differential Law

• Taenia saginata (Beef Tapeworm): Scolex has 4 suckers without rostellum or hooks; gravid proglottid has 15–30 main lateral uterine branches; active motility (crawls out of anus). Non-cysticercotic in humans.
• Taenia solium (Pork Tapeworm): Scolex has 4 suckers + armed rostellum with 2 rows of hooks; gravid proglottid has 7–13 main lateral uterine branches. Ingestion of eggs causes fatal human cysticercosis & neurocysticercosis.
• Taenia Diagnostic Egg: Spherical (\(30 ext{–}40\ \mu ext{m}\)), thick brown radially striated embryophore with 6-hooked hexacanth oncosphere.

2. Diphyllobothrium & Hymenolepis

• Diphyllobothrium latum (Broad Fish Tapeworm): Giant tapeworm (up to \(15 ext{ m}\)); scolex with 2 sucking grooves (bothria); central rosette uterus; operculated egg (\(60 ext{–}75\ \mu ext{m}\)) with abopercular knob; causes vitamin \( ext{B}_{12}\) deficiency megaloblastic anaemia.
• Hymenolepis nana (Dwarf Tapeworm): Direct cycle + internal autoinfection; oval egg (\(30 ext{–}47\ \mu ext{m}\)) with 4–8 polar filaments arising from inner membrane.

3. Liver, Intestinal & Lung Flukes

• Fasciola hepatica / gigantica: Enormous operculated eggs (\(130 ext{–}150 imes 63 ext{–}90\ \mu ext{m}\)); unembryonated; freshwater snail host (*Lymnaea*); transmitted by encysted metacercariae on watercress.
• Opisthorchis / Clonorchis sinensis: Small pitcher-shaped operculated egg (\(27 ext{–}35 imes 12 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\)) with prominent shoulder rim and terminal abopercular knob. Transmitted via raw/undercooked cyprinid fish; induces cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer).
• Paragonimus westermani: Lung fluke; operculated eggs in rust-coloured sputum or swallowed in stool; crab/crayfish transmission.

4. Enterobius Scotch Tape Protocol

Gravid female Enterobius vermicularis migrates nocturnally to perianal folds to deposit 10,000+ eggs causing intense pruritus ani. Standard faecal examination is negative; diagnosis requires clear cellulose adhesive tape (Scotch tape swab / NIH swab) pressed against perianal skin early morning. Asymmetrical plano-convex ("D-shaped") eggs (\(50 ext{–}60 imes 20 ext{–}30\ \mu ext{m}\)).

1. Trematodes (Liver, Intestinal & Lung Flukes) (Cheesbrough pp. 227–235)

Trematodes (flukes) are unsegmented, leaf-shaped hermaphroditic flatworms (except schistosomes). Life cycles involve aquatic snails as primary intermediate hosts and encysted metacercariae as the infective stage for humans:

Fluke Species Adult Habitat & Morphology Diagnostic Egg Architecture Transmission Vehicle & Clinical Pathology
Clonorchis / Opisthorchis sinensis (Chinese Liver Fluke) Biliary ducts of liver; spatulate, transparent (\(10 ext{–}25 imes 3 ext{–}5 ext{ mm}\)); highly branched dendritic testes. Small, pitcher-shaped / vase-shaped (\(27 ext{–}35 imes 12 ext{–}20\ \mu ext{m}\)); yellowish-brown; convex operculum resting on a distinct opercular shoulder rim; small abopercular knob at posterior pole. Contains fully formed miracidium. Ingestion of raw, undercooked, pickled, or dried freshwater cyprinid fish containing encysted metacercariae. Causes chronic cholangitis, biliary stone formation, and cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct carcinoma).
Fasciola hepatica & F. gigantica (Sheep / Giant Liver Fluke) Large bile ducts and liver parenchyma; large, fleshy leaf-shaped (\(20 ext{–}30 ext{ mm}\) for F. hepatica; up to \(75 ext{ mm}\) for F. gigantica) with a distinct anterior conical cone. Enormous size (\(130 ext{–}150 imes 63 ext{–}90\ \mu ext{m}\)); unembryonated; filled with unsegmented yolk cells; golden-yellow-brown thin shell with an indistinct, flat operculum. Ingestion of unwashed raw aquatic plants (especially wild watercress) harboring encysted metacercariae. Juvenile flukes burrow through Glisson's capsule causing hepatic necrosis, right upper quadrant pain, high fever, and marked eosinophilia.
Fasciolopsis buski (Giant Intestinal Fluke) Duodenum and jejunum; massive, thick fleshy fluke (\(20 ext{–}75 imes 8 ext{–}20 ext{ mm}\)); lacks anterior cephalic cone. Large, ellipsoidal (\(130 ext{–}140 imes 80 ext{–}85\ \mu ext{m}\)); golden-brown shell with a small operculum; unembryonated (virtually indistinguishable from Fasciola egg). Ingestion of raw aquatic plants (water caltrop, water chestnut, lotus roots) peeled with the teeth. Causes duodenal mucosal ulceration, malabsorption, toxic generalized oedema, and intestinal obstruction.
Heterophyes heterophyes & Metagonimus yokogawai (Minute Flukes) Small intestinal mucosa; extremely tiny flukes (\(1.0 ext{–}1.7 ext{ mm}\)); genital sucker (gonotyl). Minute operculated eggs (\(26 ext{–}30 imes 15 ext{–}17\ \mu ext{m}\)); thick light brown shell without distinct shoulders; contains miracidium. Ingestion of raw brackish water fish (mullet, tilapia). Eggs can enter mesenteric venules and embolize to heart valves (myocarditis) or brain.
Paragonimus westermani & P. africanus (Lung Fluke) Encapsulated in fibrous cysts in lung parenchyma; plump, coffee-bean shaped (\(8 ext{–}16 imes 4 ext{–}8 ext{ mm}\)). Golden-brown operculated egg (\(80 ext{–}120 imes 45 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a thickened abopercular shell end and distinct opercular collar rim. Ingestion of raw or pickled freshwater crabs or crayfish. Causes endemic haemoptysis, chronic productive cough with chocolate-brown rust-coloured sputum, cavitary lung lesions mimicking pulmonary tuberculosis. Eggs found in sputum and swallowed in faeces.

2. Cestodes (Intestinal Tapeworms) (Cheesbrough pp. 235–242)

Cestodes (tapeworms) are ribbon-like segmented hermaphroditic flatworms consisting of a head (scolex), unsegmented neck (growth zone), and a chain of progressively maturing segments (proglottids forming a strobila). They lack an alimentary tract and absorb nutrients directly across the tegument:

Tapeworm Species Scolex Morphology Gravid Proglottid Uterine Branches Diagnostic Egg Morphology Clinical Pathology & Human Cysticercosis
Taenia saginata (Beef Tapeworm) Quadrate, \(1.5 ext{–}2 ext{ mm}\); 4 hemispherical suckers; no rostellum; no hooks (unarmed). Elongated (\(16 ext{–}20 imes 5 ext{–}7 ext{ mm}\)); 15 to 30 main lateral uterine branches on each side; actively motile (crawls out of anus). Spherical / subspherical (\(31 ext{–}43\ \mu ext{m}\)); thick, yellowish-brown radially striated embryophore enclosing a 6-hooked oncosphere (hexacanth). Indistinguishable from T. solium egg. Adult worm in upper jejunum (\(4 ext{–}10 ext{ meters}\)). Humans are definitive host only. Does NOT cause human cysticercosis.
Taenia solium (Pork Tapeworm) Globular, \(1 ext{ mm}\); 4 suckers + prominent rostellum armed with a double crown of 22–32 hooks. Squarish (\(10 ext{–}12 imes 5 ext{–}6 ext{ mm}\)); 7 to 13 main lateral uterine branches on each side; non-motile (passed passively in faeces). Spherical (\(31 ext{–}43\ \mu ext{m}\)); identical to T. saginata with brown radially striated shell and 6 hooklets. Adult in jejunum (\(2 ext{–}4 ext{ meters}\)). CRITICAL DANGER: Ingestion of eggs leads to oncosphere hatching and systemic dissemination to brain, eyes, and muscles, causing Human Neurocysticercosis (epileptic seizures, intracranial hypertension, blindness, stroke).
Diphyllobothrium latum (Broad Fish Tapeworm) Elongated almond-shaped (\(2 ext{–}3 ext{ mm}\)); two deep lateral sucking slits (bothria); no hooks. Broader than long (\(3 imes 10 ext{ mm}\)); central rosette-shaped / coiled uterus; centrally placed genital pore. Broadly oval (\(58 ext{–}75 imes 40 ext{–}50\ \mu ext{m}\)); light golden-brown; distinct operculum at one pole and a small abopercular knob / papilla at the opposite pole. Unembryonated. Inhabits ileum (\(3 ext{–}15 ext{ meters}\)); transmitted by eating raw/undercooked freshwater fish (pike, salmon, trout). Adult worm selectively absorbs massive amounts of vitamin \( ext{B}_{12}\) (up to 80–100%), leading to pernicious-like megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
Hymenolepis nana (Dwarf Tapeworm) Small (\(0.3 ext{ mm}\)); 4 suckers + retractile rostellum with a single circle of 20–30 hooks. Adult measures \(15 ext{–}40 ext{ mm}\). Very tiny, broader than long; disintegrates in the bowel lumen so proglottids are rarely seen intact. Spherical / oval (\(30 ext{–}47\ \mu ext{m}\)); thin, colourless transparent outer membrane and an inner embryophore membrane with two polar thickenings from which 4 to 8 long wavy polar filaments arise, traversing the space between membranes. Encloses 6-hooked oncosphere. Most common tapeworm worldwide. Direct life cycle: no intermediate host required; capable of internal autoinfection in the bowel leading to heavy worm burdens (\(>1000\) worms) in children causing enteritis, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea.
Hymenolepis diminuta (Rat Tapeworm) Club-shaped scolex; 4 suckers; rudimentary unarmed rostellum. Adult measures \(20 ext{–}60 ext{ cm}\). Trapezoidal segments; disintegrate in bowel. Larger, round (\(60 ext{–}80\ \mu ext{m}\)); yellowish-brown thick shell; NO polar filaments. Zoonosis transmitted by accidental ingestion of flour beetles / mealmoths (*Tribolium*) in grain/cereal.
Dipylidium caninum (Double-Pored Dog Tapeworm) Conical scolex; 4 suckers + retractable rostellum with 1–7 rows of thorn-like hooks. Elongated, cucumber seed / barrel-shaped proglottids with two lateral genital pores (one on each margin). Passed in distinctive egg packets / capsules containing 5 to 30 spherical hexacanth eggs (\(35 ext{–}40\ \mu ext{m}\)). Zoonotic infection in children caused by accidental ingestion of dog/cat fleas (*Ctenocephalides canis/felis*) containing cysticercoid larvae.

3. Enterobius vermicularis (Pinworm / Threadworm) (Cheesbrough pp. 242–243)

Enterobius vermicularis is an obligate human pinworm infecting children worldwide regardless of socioeconomic status:

  • Adult Worm Morphology: Small, white, thread-like roundworm with prominent bilateral cephalic cuticular expansions (cephalic alae) and an esophageal bulb. Female measures \(8 ext{–}13 ext{ mm}\) with a long, sharply pointed pin-like posterior tail; male measures \(2 ext{–}5 ext{ mm}\) with a strongly curled tail.
  • Pathogenesis & Nocturnal Migration: Adult worms reside in the caecum, appendix, and ascending colon. At night, gravid females migrate out of the anus onto the perianal and perineal skin folds, where each female expels 10,000 to 15,000 eggs before dying. The crawling female and secretions cause intense tickling and pruritus ani, leading to scratching, excoriation, secondary bacterial infection, insomnia, restlessness, and nocturnal enuresis.
  • Transmission Dynamics:
    • Direct Anus-to-Mouth Autoinfection: Scratching deposits eggs under fingernails → transfer to mouth.
    • Retroinfection: Eggs hatch on the warm, moist perianal skin, and larvae crawl back through the anus into the colon to mature.
    • Airborne / Inhalation Transmission: Lightweight eggs contaminate bed linen, nightclothes, and house dust; eggs become airborne during bed-making and are inhaled and swallowed. Entire families must be treated simultaneously.
  • Diagnostic Scotch Tape (NIH Swab) SOP:
    • Standard faecal examinations are positive in \(<10\%\) of cases because eggs are laid externally on the skin, not in the faecal stream.
    • Procedure: Apply a strip of clear transparent cellulose adhesive tape (not frosted or opaque tape) over a wooden tongue depressor, press the sticky surface firmly against the perianal folds early in the morning before bathing or defecation, mount the tape sticky-side down onto a glass microscope slide, and examine under the \(10 imes\) objective.
  • Diagnostic Egg: Distinctive asymmetrical plano-convex ("D-shaped") appearance (\(50 ext{–}60 imes 20 ext{–}30\ \mu ext{m}\)); one side is flattened and the other is convex. Possesses a smooth, thin, colourless double-contoured transparent shell enclosing a partially or fully developed tadpole-like larva. Fully infective within 4–6 hours of oviposition.

Section 5.6 Interactive Examination Bank (8 High-Yield Clinical MCQs)

Test your mastery of fluke life cycles, tapeworm proglottid anatomy, neurocysticercosis transmission, and pinworm diagnostics:

Question 5.6.1 (Q289): A laboratory receives a tapeworm segment passed in the stool of an adult male. Examination of the cleared gravid proglottid under a dissecting microscope reveals 24 main lateral uterine branches filled with eggs on each side of the central uterine stem. The scolex recovered after purgation shows 4 hemispherical suckers with no rostellum and no hooklets. What is the definitive diagnosis?
Correct Answer: A (Taenia saginata)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 236–238 & Fig. 5.18: Taenia saginata is definitively identified by having 15 to 30 main lateral uterine branches on each side of the gravid proglottid, an unarmed scolex (4 suckers without rostellum or hooks), and active segment motility. In contrast, Taenia solium has only 7 to 13 main lateral uterine branches and an armed scolex with a double crown of hooks.
Question 5.6.2 (Q290): Why is human infection with Taenia solium considered a grave medical emergency compared to Taenia saginata infection?
Correct Answer: B (Human Neurocysticercosis from egg ingestion)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 237: Humans who ingest viable Taenia solium eggs (via contaminated food/water or autoinfection from their own adult worm) act as intermediate hosts. Oncospheres hatch in the intestine, enter the vascular system, and encyst throughout the central nervous system, eyes, and muscles as Cysticercus cellulosae (neurocysticercosis), leading to severe epilepsy, intracranial hypertension, dementia, and death. Taenia saginata eggs cannot infect humans.
Question 5.6.3 (Q291): A Scandinavian immigrant presenting with fatigue and sensory ataxia is found to have severe macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, low serum vitamin \( ext{B}_{12}\), and elevated methylmalonic acid. Stool examination reveals broad, unembryonated operculated eggs (\(65 imes 45\ \mu ext{m}\)) with a small abopercular knob at the posterior pole. What organism is responsible?
Correct Answer: C (Diphyllobothrium latum)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 238–240 & Plate 5.33: Diphyllobothrium latum (the broad fish tapeworm) lives in the ileum and selectively sequesters host dietary vitamin \( ext{B}_{12}\) (absorbing up to 80–100% of the luminal \( ext{B}_{12}\)), leading to classical hypersegmented neutrophilia, megaloblastic anaemia, and neurological subacute combined degeneration. The diagnostic eggs are golden-brown, operculated, and possess a characteristic abopercular knob / papilla at the posterior end.
Question 5.6.4 (Q292): Microscopic examination of a paediatric stool sample reveals small, colourless, spherical eggs (\(38\ \mu ext{m}\)) possessing a thin outer membrane and an inner embryophore with two prominent polar thickenings, from which 4 to 8 long wavy polar filaments radiate into the inter-membranous space. What is the diagnosis?
Correct Answer: A (Hymenolepis nana)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 240–241 & Plate 5.34: Hymenolepis nana (the dwarf tapeworm) is definitively distinguished by its characteristic egg morphology: an inner membrane surrounding the 6-hooked oncosphere with two distinct polar papillae/knobs from which 4 to 8 wavy, hair-like polar filaments project. Hymenolepis diminuta eggs lack polar filaments.
Question 5.6.5 (Q293): A 6-year-old child suffers from intense nocturnal perianal itching (pruritus ani), restlessness, and disturbed sleep. Routine direct saline and formol-ether stool examinations performed on three consecutive days are all negative for parasites. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
Correct Answer: D (Clear cellulose adhesive tape / Scotch tape swab early morning)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 243 & Plate 5.38: Gravid female Enterobius vermicularis pinworms migrate out through the anus at night to deposit eggs directly onto the perianal and perineal skin folds, not in the faeces. Consequently, standard stool examinations are positive in \(<10\%\) of cases. The gold standard diagnostic method is the Scotch cellulose adhesive tape swab applied to perianal skin in the early morning before washing.
Question 5.6.6 (Q294): An adhesive tape preparation viewed under the microscope reveals numerous characteristic asymmetrical plano-convex ("D-shaped") eggs measuring \(55 imes 25\ \mu ext{m}\) with a smooth colourless double-contoured shell enclosing a developing larva. What organism has been identified?
Correct Answer: B (Enterobius vermicularis / Pinworm)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 243 & Plate 5.38: Enterobius vermicularis eggs have a unique, unmistakable plano-convex / "D-shaped" morphology (one side flattened, the other side convex) measuring \(50 ext{–}60 imes 20 ext{–}30\ \mu ext{m}\) with a thin, transparent, colourless double shell containing a partially or fully developed tadpole-like vermiform larva.
Question 5.6.7 (Q295): In Southeast Asia, chronic biliary infection with the liver fluke Opisthorchis viverrini or Clonorchis sinensis acquired by consuming raw cyprinid freshwater fish is strongly associated with the malignant transformation of bile duct epithelium into which life-threatening neoplasm?
Correct Answer: A (Cholangiocarcinoma / Bile duct carcinoma)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 229: Chronic mechanical irritation, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, and carcinogenic excretory-secretory products from Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis dwelling in the intrahepatic biliary tree trigger adenomatous hyperplasia, chronic periductal fibrosis, and high-incidence malignant transformation into cholangiocarcinoma (Group 1 biological carcinogen).
Question 5.6.8 (Q296): A patient from the Far East with chronic cough, chest pain, and recurrent rust-coloured hemoptysis mimicking pulmonary tuberculosis has negative sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smears. Microscopic examination of the brownish sputum wet mount reveals golden-brown, operculated eggs measuring \(90 imes 55\ \mu ext{m}\) with a thickened abopercular shell wall and an opercular rim collar. What organism is responsible?
Correct Answer: C (Paragonimus westermani / Lung fluke)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 234–235: Paragonimus westermani (the lung fluke) lives encysted in pairs within pulmonary fibro-granulomatous cavities. Infection causes chronic cavitation, fibrosis, and production of characteristic gelatinous "anchovy paste" or rust-coloured sputum laden with golden-brown operculated eggs (\(80 ext{–}120 imes 45 ext{–}70\ \mu ext{m}\)). Eggs can also be swallowed and recovered in faeces.
Master Overview › Chapter 5: Parasitological Tests › 5.7 Examination of Blood for Malaria Parasites
PART 1 • CHAPTER 5 • SUBUNIT 5.7

Examination of Blood for Malaria Parasites: Species Morphology, Staining SOPs, Quantification & RDTs

Book Pages: 244–262
Section 5.7 Core Examination & Clinical Competencies (Cheesbrough pp. 244–262)

1. Thick vs Thin Film Law

• Thick Blood Film: 30 times more sensitive than a thin film; dehaemoglobinized (RBCs lysed during aqueous staining); gold standard for parasite detection and quantification.
• Thin Blood Film: Methanol-fixed (preserves intact RBC morphology); mandatory for definitive Plasmodium species identification, red cell enlargement, and stippling assessment.

2. The Giemsa Buffer pH 7.2 Rule

Giemsa and Field's staining require buffered water strictly adjusted to pH 7.1 to 7.2. If \( ext{pH} <6.8\), parasite cytoplasm stains pale grey and Schüffner's/Maurer's stippling fails to appear; if \( ext{pH} >7.4\), red blood cells stain intense blue-black, completely obscuring intracellular rings and schizonts.

3. WHO Parasitaemia Quantification

Count parasites against 200 to 500 WBCs on a thick film: \[ ext{Parasites}/\mu ext{L} = rac{ ext{Parasites Counted} imes 8000}{ ext{WBCs Counted}}\] Hyperparasitaemia threshold: \(>5\%\) infected RBCs (or \(>250,000/\mu ext{L}\)) denotes severe, life-threatening P. falciparum malaria.

4. Four Human Plasmodium Species

• P. falciparum: Multiple fine rings, double chromatin dots, appliqué forms, crescentic/banana-shaped gametocytes; schizonts sequestered in deep capillaries.
• P. vivax: Enlarged pale RBCs, amoeboid trophozoite, Schüffner's dots, 12–24 merozoite schizont.
• P. malariae: Normal/small RBCs, rectangular band forms, daisy-head rosette schizont with 6–12 merozoites.
• P. ovale: Oval enlarged RBCs with fimbriated / ragged ends, James's dots, 4–12 merozoite schizont.

1. Malaria Parasite Biology & Life Cycle Mechanics (Cheesbrough pp. 247–253)

Malaria is caused by obligate intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted by the nocturnal bite of infective female Anopheles mosquitoes (primarily Anopheles gambiae complex in Africa):

  • Exoerythrocytic (Hepatic) Schizogony: Inoculated needle-like sporozoites invade hepatocytes within 30–60 minutes. They divide asexually over 5–16 days into tissue schizonts releasing 10,000–40,000 merozoites into the circulation. In P. vivax and P. ovale, a fraction of sporozoites differentiate into dormant hypnozoites that persist for months to years, causing clinical relapses.
  • Erythrocytic Schizogony: Merozoites invade red blood cells, developing from early ring trophozoites → mature trophozoites → schizonts (multinucleated) → merozoites. RBC rupture releases pyrogens (haemozoin, GPI anchors, TNF-\(lpha\)) triggering synchronized paroxysmal chills, high fever spikes, and rigors. Periodicities: 48 hours (tertian: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale); 72 hours (quartan: P. malariae); 24 hours (quotidian: P. knowlesi).
  • Microvascular Sequestration (P. falciparum): Trophozoite and schizont-infected RBCs develop surface electron-dense protuberances (knobs) containing PfEMP-1 (P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein-1). PfEMP-1 binds host endothelial receptors (CD36, ICAM-1, chondroitin sulfate A), causing cytoadherence and microvascular clogging in brain capillaries (Cerebral Malaria), kidneys (acute tubular necrosis), and placenta (maternal anaemia and low birth weight). Because schizonts sequester in deep capillaries, mature schizonts of P. falciparum are almost never seen in peripheral blood films.

2. Blood Film Preparation, Staining Protocols & Quantification (Cheesbrough pp. 253–259)

Diagnostic accuracy relies on pristine slide preparation and strictly calibrated staining chemistry:

Staining Method Reagents & pH Requirements Fixation Protocol Diagnostic Visual Characteristics
Field's Rapid Staining Field's Stain A (methylene blue & azure in phosphate buffer) + Field's Stain B (eosin in phosphate buffer). Buffered to pH 7.1–7.2. Thick film: UNFIXED (water in stain dehaemoglobinizes RBCs).
Thin film: Fixed in absolute methanol for 1–2 minutes.		 Rapid (1 minute). Chromatin dots stain bright ruby red; cytoplasm stains clear blue; Schüffner's stippling visible in thin films; background dehaemoglobinized grey-blue.
Giemsa Staining (Gold Standard) Giemsa powder in glycerol-methanol; diluted 1:10 (10%) with buffered distilled water strictly at pH 7.1–7.2 for 10–15 min. Thick film: UNFIXED (completely dried).
Thin film: Methanol-fixed for 2–3 min.		 Superior polychromatic contrast. Chromatin stains deep red-purple; cytoplasm clear sky-blue; Schüffner's/James's/Maurer's clefts stain sharply; malarial pigment stains golden-brown to deep black.

WHO Standard Malaria Parasite Quantification SOP

1. Thick Film WBC-Based Method (Standard for Routine Labs):

Examine the thick film under the \(100 imes\) oil immersion objective. Count asexual parasites (trophozoites and schizonts; exclude gametocytes) alongside white blood cells (WBCs):

  • Count until 200 WBCs are tallied if \(\ge 10\) parasites are found.
  • If \(<10\) parasites are seen after counting 200 WBCs, continue counting up to 500 WBCs.
  • Calculate parasite density assuming standard average human WBC count of \(8000/\mu ext{L}\): \[ ext{Parasites}/\mu ext{L} = rac{ ext{Asexual Parasites Counted} imes 8000}{ ext{WBCs Counted}}\]

2. Thin Film RBC Percentage Method (For High Parasitaemia \(>1\%\)):

Count total infected RBCs per 1000 red blood cells in the monolayer:

\[ ext{Parasitaemia (\%)} = rac{ ext{Number of Infected Red Cells}}{1000 ext{ Total Red Blood Cells}} imes 100\]

Clinical Threshold: A parasitaemia of \(>5\%\) (\(>250,000/\mu ext{L}\)) indicates severe hyperparasitaemic falciparum malaria requiring immediate intravenous artesunate.

3. Comprehensive Species Differential Matrix (Cheesbrough pp. 259–262)

Definitive identification of the four human Plasmodium species on stained thin blood films:

Diagnostic Parameter Plasmodium falciparum Plasmodium vivax Plasmodium malariae Plasmodium ovale
Infected Red Blood Cell Size & Shape Normal size; normal spherical shape; unaltered colour. Enlarged (\(1.5 ext{–}2 imes\)); pale, distorted, spherical. Normal or slightly smaller / contracted; normal or darker colour. Enlarged; oval shape with fimbriated / ragged fringed margins.
Red Cell Stippling (Giemsa pH 7.2) Maurer's clefts / dots (coarse, irregular, few dark red-violet clefts in mature rings). Schüffner's dots (fine, numerous, uniform pinkish-red stippling covering entire RBC). Ziemann's stippling (extremely fine, rare dots seen only with prolonged overstaining). James's / Schüffner's dots (conspicuous, prominent, early, dark reddish-pink dots).
Trophozoite Ring Morphology Delicate, tiny fine rings (1/5th to 1/6th RBC diameter); multiple rings per cell common; double chromatin dots ("headphone" form); marginal / appliqué forms. Large, thick rings (1/3rd RBC); matures into highly irregular, sprawling amoeboid trophozoite with pseudopodial extensions and vacuole. Thick, compact, solid ring ("bird's eye" form); matures into characteristic rectangular band form / sash spanning across RBC. Compact, solid, non-amoeboid ring; rounded or oval; no pseudopodia.
Mature Schizont Morphology Sequestered in deep capillary beds; almost NEVER seen in peripheral blood (contains 8–24 tiny merozoites). Large, fills entire enlarged RBC; contains 12 to 24 merozoites (average 16) with golden-brown pigment clump. Small, compact; contains 6 to 12 merozoites (average 8) symmetrically arranged around central pigment: "Daisy-head / Rosette". Compact; fills 3/4ths of RBC; contains 4 to 12 merozoites (average 8) clustered around dark brown pigment clump.
Gametocyte Morphology Crescentic / Banana-shaped / Sausage-shaped (\(9 ext{–}14\ \mu ext{m}\)); central chromatin and pigment. Appears after 7–10 days. Large, spherical / globular; fills enlarged RBC; diffuse brown-black pigment granules. Small, spherical / ovoid; fills normal-sized RBC; abundant dark coarse pigment granules. Spherical / ovoid; fills enlarged oval RBC; coarse dark pigment.

4. Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs) (Cheesbrough pp. 252–253)

Lateral-flow immunochromatographic antigen-detection strips for peripheral point-of-care diagnosis when microscopy is unavailable:

  • Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP-2): Water-soluble protein produced exclusively by asexual stages and young gametocytes of P. falciparum. Highly sensitive. Limitation: HRP-2 persists in the patient's bloodstream for 2 to 4 weeks after complete parasite eradication, resulting in false-positive results following recent successful treatment. Also gives false negatives in parasites with pfhrp2/pfhrp3 gene deletions.
  • Parasite Lactate Dehydrogenase (pLDH): Soluble glycolytic enzyme produced only by living, viable parasites. Species-specific pLDH differentiates between P. falciparum and non-falciparum species (*P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale*). Advantage: pLDH clears rapidly from blood within 24 to 48 hours of effective antimalarial therapy, making it ideal for monitoring treatment efficacy and drug resistance.
  • Pan-Malarial Aldolase: Conserved glycolytic enzyme present in all four human Plasmodium species.

Section 5.7 Interactive Examination Bank (8 High-Yield Clinical MCQs)

Test your diagnostic competence on malaria thin film microscopy, Giemsa buffer physics, WHO quantification algorithms, and RDT kinetics:

Question 5.7.1 (Q297): A Giemsa-stained thin blood film from a febrile comatose patient reveals normal-sized red blood cells containing delicate, tiny ring trophozoites with double chromatin dots ("headphone" configuration), multiple rings inside single red cells, and crescentic, banana-shaped gametocytes. Notably, no schizonts are observed in the entire film. What is the diagnosis and the pathological reason for the absence of schizonts?
Correct Answer: B (P. falciparum with deep microvascular sequestration via PfEMP-1)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 248–250 & Plate 5.43: Plasmodium falciparum is characterized by delicate rings, double chromatin dots, multiple parasitized RBCs, and crescentic (banana-shaped) gametocytes. Late-stage trophozoites and schizonts produce membrane knobs containing PfEMP-1, which mediate cytoadherence to capillary endothelium in the brain, kidneys, and placenta (sequestration), preventing circulating schizonts from appearing in peripheral blood films.
Question 5.7.2 (Q298): A laboratory technologist prepares Giemsa stain using distilled water from a container that has absorbed atmospheric carbon dioxide, lowering the water pH to \(6.2\). What severe diagnostic defect will be observed on the stained malaria blood films?
Correct Answer: A (Pale cytoplasm and absent stippling due to acidic pH)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 256: Giemsa staining is extremely pH-sensitive. If the buffer is acidic (\( ext{pH} <6.8\)), the basic azure/methylene blue dyes fail to bind properly; parasite cytoplasm stains faint grey/pale or invisible, and diagnostic red cell stippling (Schüffner's, James's, Maurer's dots) does not develop. Buffered water must be strictly maintained at pH 7.1 to 7.2 for optimal differential polychromatic staining.
Question 5.7.3 (Q299): On a thick blood film stained with Giemsa, a technologist counts 125 Plasmodium falciparum asexual ring trophozoites while counting 200 white blood cells (WBCs). Assuming the standard WHO average human WBC count of \(8000/\mu ext{L}\), what is the calculated parasite density per microliter of blood?
Correct Answer: C (\(5,000/\mu ext{L}\))
Cheesbrough Reference p. 258: According to the standard WHO thick film calculation formula: \[ ext{Parasites}/\mu ext{L} = rac{ ext{Asexual Parasites Counted} imes 8000}{ ext{WBCs Counted}} = rac{125 imes 8000}{200} = 125 imes 40 = 5,000/\mu ext{L}\]
Question 5.7.4 (Q300): Stained thin film examination of a patient with recurring 72-hour fever paroxysms reveals normal-sized to slightly smaller, dark red blood cells containing compact, solid trophozoites that form a broad rectangular "band form" / sash spanning across the entire erythrocyte. Mature schizonts display 8 merozoites arranged symmetrically around a central mass of coarse brown-black pigment ("daisy-head / rosette"). What is the species?
Correct Answer: B (Plasmodium malariae)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 260–261 & Plate 5.46: Plasmodium malariae causes quartan malaria (72-hour cycle), invades older mature RBCs (which appear normal or slightly shrunken/compact), and forms characteristic rectangular band forms or "bird's eye" rings. Its mature schizont characteristically forms a daisy-head / rosette of 6–12 merozoites (average 8) clustered around a central coarse dark pigment mass.
Question 5.7.5 (Q301): A thin blood film shows distinctly enlarged, pale red blood cells with irregular, oval contours and fimbriated, ragged, fringed edges. The infected erythrocytes exhibit prominent, dark reddish-pink James's stippling and contain compact, non-amoeboid schizonts with 8 merozoites. What organism is present?
Correct Answer: D (Plasmodium ovale)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 261 & Plate 5.45: Plasmodium ovale infects reticulocytes, causing infected RBCs to become oval-shaped with characteristic ragged, fimbriated (fringed) edges. It shows heavy, conspicuous, early James's (Schüffner's) stippling and compact, non-amoeboid trophozoites with schizonts containing 4–12 merozoites (average 8). In contrast, P. vivax RBCs are enlarged and round with highly amoeboid trophozoites and 12–24 merozoites.
Question 5.7.6 (Q302): A patient successfully treated for acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria 3 weeks ago undergoes a follow-up test. The HRP-2 based Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) remains positive, but an expert thick and thin blood film examination reveals zero malaria parasites (NPF). What explains this discrepancy?
Correct Answer: B (Persistent circulating HRP-2 antigen post-treatment)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 252–253: Plasmodium falciparum Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP-2) has a long half-life and remains detectable in host circulation for 2 to 4 weeks (or longer) after successful antimalarial therapy has killed all asexual parasites. Therefore, HRP-2 RDTs cannot differentiate between active infection and recently cured infection. In contrast, pLDH tests clear within 24–48 hours and reflect true parasite viability.
Question 5.7.7 (Q303): Why must blood films for malaria diagnosis include an unfixed thick blood film in addition to a fixed thin film?
Correct Answer: A (30-fold concentration and RBC lysis for low parasitaemia detection)
Cheesbrough Reference p. 253: In a thick film, multiple layers of red blood cells are dried without chemical fixation. When aqueous Giemsa or Field's stain is applied, the red cells lyse (dehaemoglobinize), leaving all concentrated malaria parasites, white cells, and platelets in a small microscopic area. This increases diagnostic sensitivity roughly 30 times compared to a thin smear monolayer.
Question 5.7.8 (Q304): Which human malaria species forms dormant hepatic stages known as hypnozoites that persist within parenchymal liver cells, requiring radical cure with primaquine to prevent recurrent clinical relapses?
Correct Answer: C (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale)
Cheesbrough Reference pp. 248, 251: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale produce latent secondary exoerythrocytic stages (hypnozoites) that remain dormant inside liver cells for months to years. Reactivation causes clinical relapses. Blood schizonticides (chloroquine, artemisinins) kill only erythrocytic stages; an 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine or tafenoquine) is required to eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites (radical cure, after checking for G6PD deficiency).
